# Preface.

## Highly Favorable Reader.

It is said in a very common, yet truthful proverb, that all is not gold that glitters. If this ever holds true, it applies above all others primarily to <term>Alchemy</term><note>original: "Alchymie." The historical practice of proto-chemistry aimed at the transmutation of base metals into gold and the discovery of a universal cure.</note>; for through the luster of the yellow metal one hopes for, as depicted by deceivers, the eyes of those <term>greedy for gold</term><note>original: "Gold-begierigen." Refers to people driven by the desire for wealth through alchemy rather than scientific or spiritual pursuits.</note> are so blinded that they do not perceive—until this deceptive appearance suddenly vanishes with the greatest dismay through the black cavern of an empty and completely exhausted purse—that this luster was rather a shadow of a futile hope, and indeed, often even a thick darkness of the mind.

To demonstrate this somewhat more extensively, I cannot help but sincerely communicate the following from my own experience to the highly favorable reader. I have diligently applied myself to <term>Chemistry</term><note>original: "Chymie." In the early 18th century, the terms chemistry and alchemy were often used interchangeably, though "Chymistry" increasingly referred to the practical laboratory work.</note> for 34 years, and previously served for 6 years under His Excellency, the Count of <term>Hohenlohe</term><note>The House of Hohenlohe was a prominent noble German family; many such nobles sponsored private laboratories and alchemists during this period.</note> and Lord...

<summary>In this preface, the author warns the reader against the deceptive allure of alchemy, comparing the empty promises of "gold-makers" to a glittering facade that leads to financial ruin. He establishes his credibility by citing over three decades of practical experience in the chemical arts and his service to the nobility.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, deception, greed, chemistry, Count of Hohenlohe, preface, experience</keywords>

[He] may be spared from the *mercurial*, *arsenical*, and *antimonial* fumes, and be secured against their poisoning and infiltration—from which many, in their old age, must finally *die*<note>original: "crepiren." A blunt term often used for the death of animals, implying a miserable or undignified passing.</note> miserably in poverty and with unhealthy bodies. Truly, in my many years of *labors*<note>original: "Laboribus." Refers to laboratory experiments and chemical work.</note>, more than 300 such people have come to me; consequently, I have not lacked for such self-proclaimed artists, as His High-Countly *Excellency* spared no expense, and yet nothing profitable was ever *effected*<note>original: "effectuiret."</note>. I would exclude one single *example*: when in the year 1704 a true *adept*<note>original: "Adeptus." A master of the alchemical art who has successfully discovered the secret of transmutation.</note> called on me to see my new gold glaze, but he, with a few words, brought me to the point where I can say: Praise be to God! This *story*<note>original: "Historia."</note> can be read in the newly appointed *Agent* of the first *function*, 9th *dispatch*<note>original: "Depeche."</note>, *page* 838. But because my manifold *labors* do not allow me to investigate this secret, I must remain in patience until it might please God. 

After this, I have completely *abandoned*<note>original: "abandonniret."</note> alchemy and, in the meantime, loved pure *chemistry*, practicing it with the greatest care and diligence. Furthermore—without wishing to mention any vain glory—I have discovered many a fine *science* and highly useful *techniques*<note>original: "Encheirefes," from the Greek "Encheiresis." Refers to manual operations or specific laboratory procedures.</note>, among which I have also come to know the Philosophers’ **green and red lions**<note>Alchemical symbols: the "Green Lion" often refers to vitriol or antimony used as a solvent, while the "Red Lion" typically represents the final stage of the Philosophers' Stone or a specific metallic oxide.</note> very well, as shown in the first copperplate engraving. Likewise, through the noble *art of separation*<note>original: "Scheide-Kunst." Metallurgical assaying and refining.</note>, I have learned how to *separate* gold from silver in the "dry way" without *aqua fortis*<note>original: "Aqua fort." Nitric acid, the standard solvent used in the "wet way" to dissolve silver and leave gold behind.</note>. My newly invented **gold glaze**, the like of which has never been seen or thought of by any man before, shall serve as proof of this. For this reason, I have also had the high grace that four Royal Majesties and, most recently, His *Czarist Majesty*<note>Likely Peter the Great, who took a keen interest in European technology and chemistry during his travels.</note> most graciously deigned to come to my house to inspect it personally, wondered at it, and observed it with great *satisfaction*<note>original: "Contentement."</note>. # Preface

<meta>catchword: After-</meta>

To come a bit closer to my present purpose: as I lived for about 21 years away from my *homeland*<note>original: "Patria."</note>, namely Leipzig, I once became closely *acquainted* with a man of a religious order while traveling, who was also a great lover of chemistry. This same man gave me this beautiful book, the *Precious Pearl*<note>original: "Margaritam pretiosam." This refers to the *Pretiosa Margarita Novella* (The New Precious Pearl), an influential alchemical treatise written by Petrus Bonus of Ferrara in the 14th century.</note>, as a keepsake. Since this book is now almost impossible to find and is so rare that it cannot even be found in several very famous libraries—and was published more than a century and a half ago under the high *privileges*<note>original: "Privilegiis." Legal protections or licenses granted by authorities, similar to a modern copyright or patent.</note> of Pope *Paul* III and the Council of Venice—I have had it translated into German for the sake of the German *nation* and brought it to light once more. I also wished to remedy the current lack of Latin *copies* with a sufficient supply of German ones, so that those who are not skilled in the Latin language may use it for their benefit in the same way. As I in no way doubt that many will be able to take something good from it—because it very easily teaches the correct *preparation of the Blessed Stone*<note>original: "præparationem Lapidis Benedicti." A devotional name for the Philosopher's Stone, the substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and curing all diseases.</note> from beginning to end, in a way that can be found in almost no other book—it will be well worth the expenses incurred and the great effort to bring this noble book, which has lain as if in a grave for so long, back into the light. For I wish that God may grant that it provides much benefit to pious lovers [of the art] and artists, and that they may receive the true light from it! Meanwhile, may the highly favored reader fare well, and use it for God's praise and honor, as well as for the service and benefit of one's neighbor.

Given at Leipzig, April 16, 1714.

->**Wolffgang Georg Stoll.**<-

<summary>Wolfgang Georg Stoll explains how he acquired a rare copy of the "Precious Pearl" from a monk and decided to translate it from Latin into German to make its secrets regarding the Philosopher's Stone accessible to a wider audience.</summary>
<keywords>Wolfgang Georg Stoll, Leipzig, Margarita Pretiosa, Precious Pearl, Petrus Bonus, Pope Paul III, Venice, Latin translation, Blessed Stone, Philosopher's Stone, alchemy history</keywords>

--- Page 34 ---
<meta>This page follows the title page of the 1714 German edition. It contains two short dedicatory or introductory statements by Pierius Roseus, a name associated with the editing of this collection, praising both the medicinal and material benefits of the alchemical secrets contained within.</meta>

## Pierius Roseus to the sincere
### Reader.

This work banishes from the human body that sickness which senseless anger is accustomed to arouse; and it teaches how one may preserve youth in its most beautiful bloom, and one day behold a peaceful old age. If anyone, through divine assistance, carries out its commands, he will with joy banish all poverty that he outwardly shows. As long as he lives here, he will be able to provide assistance to the poor and needy, and thank the great God in humility for the grace <note>In an alchemical context, "grace" often refers to the "Donum Dei" or Gift of God—the successful creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> bestowed upon him.

### By the same author.

To all those who have practiced this art <note>The "Art" refers to alchemy, specifically the "Great Work" of transmutation and healing.</note> before now, our Calabrian <note>original: "Calabrier." This refers to Janus Lacinus, the monk from Calabria who originally compiled the anthology.</note> gives this as a reward for their great labor: he bids them to step back. 
Do you see here a diligence that yields gold? Marvel at it, and firmly believe that he who does not possess this book, possesses nothing.

<meta>catchword: The</meta>

<summary>This preface by Pierius Roseus praises the book’s ability to heal the body, extend youth, and provide enough wealth to eliminate poverty and help the needy. It concludes by asserting that this specific compilation by Janus Lacinus is superior to all previous alchemical texts.</summary>

<keywords>Pierius Roseus, Janus Lacinus, health, longevity, poverty, charity, alchemy as divine gift, superiority of the text</keywords>

--- Page 35 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory front matter of the 1714 edition. Following Pierius Roseus’s praise of the editor Janus Lacinius, this page features a poem by Hippolytus Fantotius. The "catchword" from the previous page, "The" (or "Der" in German), likely referred to the start of the title or the next section; here the catchword "Janus" points toward the central figure of the editor.</meta>

# A poem composed concerning this book by
# Hippolytus Fantotius of Perugia in
## Dauphiné.

I, as a divine art <note>In this poem, Alchemy speaks in the first person, a literary device known as prosopopoeia.</note>, have for a long time endured an unjust servitude under wicked masters, and have lain sighing, hidden beneath darkness as thick as a post. As I now strive to step swiftly once more before highly learned and experienced men, and implore many for their help and assistance in this matter, wretched people delay it from one season to the next. At last, only Lacinius <note>Janus Lacinius, the Calabrian monk and editor of this collection.</note> takes pity on me, for my tears and miserable state touch his heart; he strips away my filth and unseemly rags, and clothes me in handsome adornment. And by placing a bright light before the eyes of all, he shows what the diligence of this mighty art is capable of. 

Therefore, you, kind reader, may see what understanding and skill I have bestowed upon this man. He presents anew, in a very brief method of instruction, that which Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–c. 815), the most influential figure in early Islamic and European alchemy.</note>, Bonus <note>Petrus Bonus, the 14th-century author of the *Precious New Pearl*, whose work is a cornerstone of this collection.</note>, and even Raymond <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many foundational alchemical texts were attributed.</note> himself—who devoted himself most particularly to this art—described in so many books. This learned man, through whose diligence I have once again come among the learned, is truly worthy of the highest honor.

<summary>In this poem, the personified "Art of Alchemy" laments its previous neglect and corruption by ignorant teachers until being rescued and refined by the editor Janus Lacinius. The text credits Lacinius with distilling the vast, difficult works of Geber, Petrus Bonus, and Raymond Lull into a concise and clear format.</summary>

<keywords>Alchemy personified, Hippolytus Fantotius, Janus Lacinius, Geber, Petrus Bonus, Raymond Lull, alchemical lineage, restoration of knowledge</keywords>

--- Page 36 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory matter of the 1714 edition of Janus Lacinius’s alchemical collection. The previous page concluded a poem by Hippolytus Fantotius, which personified the "divine art" of alchemy as a woman rescued from rags and obscurity by Lacinius. This page begins Lacinius’s own preface, where he addresses the reader directly, using a philosophical argument about virtue and vice to justify his decision to publish these secret works for the public good.</meta>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut header at the top of the page features ornate acanthus leaf scrolls on the left and right. In the center is a circular medallion or wreath containing a symbol of a stylized flame or torch with radiant lines extending outwards.</image-desc>

# Janus Lacinius, a Minorite <note>A member of the Order of Friars Minor, also known as the Franciscans.</note> from Calabria, wishes the gracious reader happiness and salvation!

Gracious Reader! Because contrary things (according to the testimony of the Philosopher <note>original: "Philoſophi." In this context, "The Philosopher" almost always refers to Aristotle, whose logic dictated that opposites are better understood when compared side-by-side.</note>) must be discussed at the same time, so that when they are placed side-by-side, they might strike the eye more clearly: For this reason, the virtue of generosity is not so much to be praised and strived for, as the vice of greed is rather to be declared shameful and utterly cursed. 

For just as those who consider that they were born into the light of this world not so much for themselves, but rather for the benefit of their fatherland and all upright friends—those who apply not only their effort and diligence but also all their means for the common good of honest people—are rightly esteemed as worthy of all honor: So, on the other hand, are those who, out of pride and an immoderate desire to acquire more and more—forgetting all justice and their human condition—bury their treasures in the earth, are intent only upon their own profit, and solely and exclusively 

<summary>Janus Lacinius begins his preface by arguing that the virtue of generosity is best understood when contrasted with the vice of greed. He praises those who share their knowledge and wealth for the common good, setting the stage for his decision to publish alchemical secrets.</summary>

# Dedicatory Dialogue between Bonus and Lacinius.

->Bonus.<-

My Lacinius, all those who have written something excellent and remarkable in all kinds of arts and sciences—or have newly revised, improved, and expanded them—have hitherto been accustomed to allowing such works to be issued in public print for the general benefit of the lovers <note>In this context, "lovers" refers to "amateurs" or "devotees" of a particular field of study.</note> of these subjects, so that posterity might also draw an advantage from them. A reference to Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> and others. A literal translation of Alchemy.</note>.

### Explanation of the Obscure Images

There are three things to be well observed in this work: First, prepare the <term>matter<gloss>The physical substance or base material used in the alchemical process</gloss></term> well; secondly, proceed diligently with the work so that it is not hindered by an interruption of its progress; thirdly, be patient and observe the most certain fundamental principles of nature in all things. 

Initially, prepare the magnificent <term>Water of Life<gloss>Known in Latin as "Aqua Vitae," this is a potent spirit or solvent considered essential to the alchemical "Great Work"</gloss></term>, purify it, and store it carefully. Do not doubt, however, that this juice—with which everything is moistened—is indeed the pure and bright moisture of <term>Bacchus<gloss>The Roman god of wine; here symbolizing a spiritual or alcoholic essence or "mercurial" spirit</gloss></term> <note>original: "Bacchi"</note>. For if you linger and lose your way in various matters through countless impassable places, you will overlook this blessed water. 

When you then enter the palace, which contains fifteen rooms, you will see the King in his crown upon an exalted throne, holding the scepter of the whole world in his hand. Before his majesty, his son and five servants, dressed in various kinds of <term>livery<gloss>Specific uniforms that often represent different chemical states, metallic properties, or planetary associations</gloss></term>, fall to their knees and plead with the King to deign to share his kingdom with both the son and the servants. To this petition, however, the King gives no answer.

[An engraving illustrating the text. On the left, a king (labeled <note>original: "Rex"</note> **King** on the throne's headrest) sits on a high, ornate throne holding a long scepter. The word <note>original: "ORO"</note> **I PRAY** is inscribed on his lap. On the right, six figures kneel in prayerful supplication before him. One figure in front is designated as the son (labeled <note>original: "filius"</note> **son** at the bottom right), followed by five servants in similar dress.]

<summary>This page provides instructions for the early stages of alchemical work, emphasizing the preparation of the "Water of Life" and introducing an allegory of a King and his six petitioners.</summary>

<note>This violent allegory represents the chemical "death" or breakdown of a solid substance—the "Old King"—to release its inner essence. The servants often represent the different chemical agents or planetary influences that assist in this transformation.</note>

<meta>This page follows the Ninth Chamber, where the remains were removed from the grave. It details the transition from the black stage of putrefaction (*nigredo*) to the white stage of purification (*albedo*), using the "Tenth Chamber" as a metaphor for a specific chemical distillation and washing process.</meta>

<page-num>37</page-num>
<sig>E 3</sig>

<image-desc>An etching depicts a man kneeling in a barren, rocky landscape, holding a mallet or heavy tool in his right hand. Before him on the ground lie scattered human skeletal remains, including long bones and a prominent skull.</image-desc>

In the tenth chamber, the bones are divided into nine parts; this occurs when the dissolved matter is cooked for nine days over a gentle fire until it takes on a black color. When this has been removed again, place it in another vessel in a warm location and boil out the water once more for nine days; and if you find that it has turned black, collect it and set it aside with the other. You must continue in this manner until the water is bright and pure. The <term>putrefaction<gloss>The stage of decomposition and blackening, known as *nigredo*</gloss></term>, however, or the blackness, should be put into a glass vessel, and some of its <term>Water of Life<gloss>In alchemy, *Aqua Vitae*; a potent solvent or distilled spirit used to "animate" the dead matter</gloss></term> should be added to it, so that it covers it by a finger's breadth. It should thereafter be cooked over a gentle fire for nine days, and where it may be necessary, fresh water should be poured over it every day. In this way, the earth will become pure and white, according to the saying of the Sages; for this earth decays with its water and is thus purified.

Thereupon an angel is sent, who throws the bones onto the purified and white earth, which is now mixed with its seed; this is now placed entirely into a completely sealed vessel with its <term>Alembic<gloss>The cap or hood of a distilling apparatus, used to collect and condense vapors</gloss></term>. After the matter has been made a little thicker, it shall be separated from the water by a stronger fire and become hard on the bottom.

# Newly-discovered precious Pearl, gathered from the writings of the Sages concerning the treasure and the Stone of the Wise; and it is a hidden work, a secret of all secrets and a Divine gift;
->brought to light by<-
## *Petrus Bonus* of *Ferrara*. <note>Petrus Bonus was a 14th-century physician. This work, the *Margarita Pretiosa Novella*, is one of the most significant texts attempting to reconcile alchemy with the philosophy of Aristotle.</note>

Because not only the ancients, but also the modern *philosophers* <note>original: *Philosophi*; at this time, "philosopher" referred to anyone studying the deep laws of nature, including alchemists</note>, who have strived to investigate the secrets of nature and their true constitution, are accustomed to investigating and disputing: Whether the art of making gold, which assists nature, is both clearly proven and simultaneously to be found in the world? Or whether it is only written and spoken of, even though it is not to be encountered in the world? Therefore, for this reason, we wish to investigate this question as well—and not superficially, as has been the custom until now, but looking very deeply and clearly, so that every scholar can recognize from the reasons cited which opinion he should join, and whether he should dedicate his diligence to this magnificent art or not. Most *physicians* <note>original: *Physici*; meaning natural scientists or those who study the physical world</note> and worldly-wise men, who have neither doubted for valid reasons nor thoroughly investigated the matter, but have only looked at it superficially, have disputed it and reached a conclusion: Some have stated that it is indeed grounded in truth; others have held it to be a deception, but none of them understood the matter, nor were they able to carry it out, even if they testified to the truth. Some among the alchemists, such as *Geber* <note>Abu Musa Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in chemistry</note> and *Morienus* <note>A legendary hermit alchemist of the 7th century</note>, have also disputed this question in their alchemical books as men who were equal to the task, though very briefly and unclearly. Against this, they presented many *arguments* <note>original: *Argumenta*</note> and refuted them; but when they were supposed to prove it, they only cited a few examples through flowery and figurative speech, answered with "Yes," and simply—

# The Newly-Discovered Precious Pearl, collected from the writings of the Sages concerning the treasure and the Stone of the Sages / and it is a hidden work / a secret of all secrets and a divine gift;
### brought to light by
## *Petrus Bonus of Ferrara.*

Because not only the ancients / but also the more recent philosophers <note>original: "Philosophi"</note>, who have labored to explore the secrets of nature and her true constitution / are accustomed to investigate and debate: Whether the art of making gold / which assists nature / has both been clearly proven / and can also be found in the world at the same time? Or whether one has only written and spoken of it / while it is actually not to be encountered in the world? Therefore, for this reason, we also wish to investigate this question / and not superficially / as has been the custom until now / but looking very deeply and clearly / so that every scholar may recognize from the cited reasons which opinion he should favor / and whether he should dedicate his diligence to this magnificent art or not. Most physicists <note>original: "Physici"; here meaning natural scientists or those who study the physical laws of nature.</note> and philosophers / who have neither doubted for weighty reasons / nor thoroughly investigated the matter / but have only looked at it superficially / have debated the subject and reached a conclusion: Some have established that it is indeed grounded in truth; others have held it to be a fraud / yet none of them understood the matter / nor were they able to carry it out / even if they testified to the truth. Some among the alchemists / such as Geber <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–813 AD), a foundational figure in alchemy.</note> and Moriemus <note>Also known as Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note>, have also debated this question in their alchemical books / as people who were equal to the task / yet only very briefly and unclearly. They brought forth many arguments against it and refuted them; but when they were supposed to prove it / they only provided a few examples through flowery and figurative speech / answering with "yes" and simply—

<meta>This page continues the introduction from page 41. The first word "simply" [original: dings] completes the phrase "schlechterdings" [simply/absolutely] from the previous page's final sentence, where the author began discussing whether alchemy is grounded in truth.</meta>

<page-num>42</page-num>
<header>(0)</header>

simply stated, that the art is indeed founded in truth. Since we therefore know something of *alchemy* <note>original: "Alchymie"</note> from its technical terms <note>original: "Terminis"</note> and the sayings of the ancient sages who have spoken truly, we wish, with the help of God, to take up this doubt-filled science in a proper manner, as we intend to reveal it through a detailed explanation and divide it into specific and orderly chapters. First, we will put forward arguments <note>original: "Argumenta"</note> against this science. Second, we will explain the art itself with proper clarity. Third, with God's assistance, we will respond to the objections brought forward by the opposing side.

It should be noted here beforehand that when the subject handled in an art or science—and its particular characteristics—are known and revealed to all, or at least to most scholars, they require no further investigation or proof, but only an explanation. If, however, such things are unknown and not revealed, then they require no further investigation or proof, but only an explanation. <note>The original German text contains a repetition of this phrase, likely a printing or transcription error.</note> But if such things are unknown and not revealed, one first requires a thorough investigation and proof, then a correct explanation, and finally certain tests, especially if their end goal results in a practical operation <note>original: "Operation"</note> and effect, so that the tests may confirm the previously established teachings. Because the subject of this art—namely whether its particular characteristics are true or false—is not entirely known or revealed, and indeed seems quite foreign to most sages, it is certainly necessary to investigate, prove, and explain it, so that the truth may be thoroughly researched. This is done so that if anything plausible should appear that might accuse the art of falsehood, it may be refuted and set aside; for every science or art, whether it be *medicine* <note>original: "Medicin"</note> or another, carries with it its own particular doubts and answers, without which the art cannot reach perfection.

There are, however, three kinds of arts, as in the second book...

--- Page 84 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 42, completing the sentence regarding the classification of arts according to Aristotle's natural philosophy.</meta>

<page-num>43</page-num>
->❁ (o) ❁<-

...which is mentioned in Aristotle's *Physics* <note>original: "Physicorum Aristotelis"; referring to the Greek philosopher’s influential works on the nature of the physical world</note>, which either prepare matter for a specific purpose, bring something into a certain form and shape, or are dedicated to common use. However, the art of making gold <note>original: "Gold zu machen"; alchemy</note> is not included among these, because it is not a mere craft <note>original: "Handwerck"</note>. But if this were granted, it would simultaneously teach how to prepare the matter and produce a certain form, yet not those things that belong to common, everyday use. For it teaches how one should truly recognize the matter that belongs to the preparation of this work <note>The "Great Work" or Magnum Opus of alchemy</note> and excludes everything else that does not pertain to it. Moreover, it shows the way and manner in which one should prepare such matter for something specific and bring it into a certain form, provided the matter is suitable for it. All of this an experienced artist recognizes and performs, and he may make use of it as he pleases, or not. 

Next to these, there are also other sciences that do not arise from mere artifice alone but are rather natural in character, such as medicine <note>original: "Medicin"</note>, the art of planting and grafting, the manufacturing of minerals, and glass-making. So far as these are practiced by humans, they can certainly be counted among the arts; but so far as a certain form is brought into such things, they arise purely from nature. For those things whose forms and effects are natural arise from nature itself. It is the same with the art of making gold. Therefore <note>original: "Ergo"</note>. There is also another kind of arts that deal with things not actually found in the world, but rather invented by human intellect, such as grammar <note>original: "Grammatica"</note>, logic <note>original: "Logica"</note>, and rhetoric <note>original: "Rhetorica"</note>; our art is not included among these. 

And because in the learning of all arts, theory <note>original: "Theoria"</note> and diligent investigation must necessarily precede actual practice <note>original: "Praxi"</note> and execution, this must also be observed here. For the end goal of theoretical investigation is the truth, which we now intend to fathom first of all. ...it is said that the art is indeed founded in truth. Initially, we want to present **arguments** <note>original: "Argumenta"</note> against this science. Secondly, we want to explain the art itself with proper clarity. Thirdly, we want, with God’s assistance, to respond to the objections brought by the opposing side.

It should be noted immediately that if the subject matter treated in an art or science—and its particular properties—is known and obvious to all, or at least to most scholars, then it requires no further investigation or proof, but only an explanation. However, if such things are unknown and not obvious, they require no further investigation or proof, but only an explanation. <note>The original text contains a repetition here that mistakenly suggests unknown things need no proof; the author corrects this logic in the very next sentence.</note> But if such things are unknown and not obvious, one first requires a thorough investigation and proof, then a correct explanation, and finally certain tests, if their goal results in an **operation** and effect, insofar as the tests confirm the previously established teachings. Since, therefore, the subject matter of this art—namely whether it be true or false along with its specific properties—is not altogether known and obvious, and indeed seems quite foreign to most sages, it is certainly necessary to investigate, prove, and explain it. This is so that the truth may be thoroughly explored, and if anything deceptive should appear that would accuse it of falsehood, it may be refuted and set aside. For every science or art, be it **medicine** or any other, carries with it its own particular doubts and answers, without which the art cannot reach perfection.

...follows, as is to be found in the second book of *Metaphysics* <note>original: "Metaphysicæ"</note> and in the 6th book of Aristotle’s *Ethics* <note>original: "Ethicorum Aristotelis"</note>, because the **practice** <term>operation; the physical labor or application of a science</term> is that which we desire after **theoretical contemplation** <term>speculation; the intellectual study of principles</term>, and because the latter is not made perfect without the former.

Note that the Philosopher <note>A common title for Aristotle in medieval and early modern texts.</note> teaches this very method of investigating a matter in the first book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de Anima"</note>; and the reason for this is that in such a way we arrive at a thorough knowledge of a thing. Hence he also says in the second book of the *Posterior [Analytics]* <note>original: "Lib. 2. posteriorum"; Aristotle's work on logic and demonstration</note>: All questions are posed concerning that thing which, once known, decides the entire question. However, that which one asks for is the **cause**, or the **means** <note>original: "Mittel"; in Aristotelian logic, this refers to the "middle term" of a syllogism which links a subject to its properties</note>, as he speaks in the cited place. Therefore, if one has well understood the "means" of the question regarding this art, then the question itself can be properly established.

* Note here further that the causes or means are of several kinds, namely:
(1) such that one can grasp with the intellect alone.
(2) actual ones, or those which can also be perceived with the external senses.
(3) natural ones, and 
(4) those produced by art <note>meaning human skill or technology</note>.

Thus, it seems to be an irrational act if someone intends to proceed to the **practice** <term>operation</term> in a matter unless the investigation of the causes and the means has preceded it. In like manner, one labors in vain if one wishes to set a certain goal for the inquiry of this art before one has properly recognized the means of such an inquiry; for no one can determine a goal for any question unless they first recognize the means, or arrive at a thorough knowledge of it through diligent searching. Those who do not know the "means" cannot decide the question, because they do not recognize the cause for which the investigation should be conducted. Whoever knows how to properly apply their doubts can also explore the matter well, and consequently perform the **practice** <term>operation</term> well; on the other hand, whoever does not know how to observe such things will not be able to succeed in the practice itself. In impossible things, it is impossible to accomplish anything. For impossible things cannot be investigated, because one has no **supporting arguments** <term>proofs; logical foundations</term> for them.

<header>Objections against the Art.</header>

# Now follow the arguments of Bonus <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century physician and alchemist from Ferrara known for defending the "Art" of alchemy against its critics.</note> against the objections of the opposition.

Because the ancients had the habit of refuting the objections brought against a science before treating it in detail, we also wish to follow them in this regard.

### The first objection.

For he who does not know the certain and determined quantity of each element within a being mixed from many parts does not know how he should produce such a mixed being. The Alchemists do not know this regarding the metals and other related parts. Therefore, etc. <note>original: "Ergo &c."; the standard conclusion of a logical syllogism.</note> The **major premise** <term>Major; the first, general proposition of a logical argument</term> is clear, because such a science is known and certain only according to its own nature—not according to what concerns us, who only know something of it in a very confused and general way. This also occurs in all other sciences that have a mixture as their basis. The **minor premise** <term>Minor; the second, specific proposition of a logical argument</term> seems to be known from what we have before us; for the metals and other related pieces belong to those mixed things upon which the alchemists still labor <note>original: "laboriren"; to work on or manipulate in a laboratory setting.</note>.

### The second objection.

Likewise, he who does not know the precisely defined proportion of the elements to one another when they are to be mixed, nor the way and manner in which they should be mixed and brought to **digestion** <term>a process of slow, constant heat used to mature a substance, similar to natural incubation</term>—through which one must obtain the form <note>The "Form" in Aristotelian philosophy is the essential nature or identity that makes a thing what it is.</note> of the mixed being—does not know how to compose such a mixed being. The Alchemists are such people, etc. Therefore. The major premise can be proven from this: because every thing in particular has its own very special form, from which its certain virtues, properties, and effects follow; and it is through this form or shape that it is [set apart] from all other things—

### The sixth objection.

Likewise, those effects which are to be attributed to nature alone cannot arise from art. The generation of metals is to be attributed to nature alone, etc. <note>original: "zc." abbreviation for "et cetera"</note> Therefore <note>original: "Ergò"</note>. The **major premise** <term>Major: the first part of a logical argument</term> is clear, because generation and transformation <note>original: "Verwechslung"; here referring to the transmutation or changing of one substance into another</note> arise from an internal **principle** <term>Principio: a fundamental source or cause</term>. This internal principle <note>original: "Principium"</note> is nature, which works the essential forms of things. Art, however, is an external principle, which is occupied only with external things, in the manner of a transformation.

In the same way, nature produces things through the mixing of the **elements** <term>Elementen: the classical four elements of earth, water, air, and fire</term>; such mixing, however, arises solely and alone from the work of the highest and most praised God and nature herself, as **Galen** <note>original: "Galenus"; a famous Greek physician and philosopher whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> speaks in his first book *On Temperaments* <note>original: "de Complexionibus"</note>. The **minor premise** <term>Minor: the second part of a logical argument</term> is proven because metals are produced from an internal principle, namely by nature, through generation and decay <note>original: "Verwesung"; in alchemy, the necessary breakdown of a substance before it can be reborn in a higher form</note> by means of a mixing.

### The seventh objection.

Likewise, if that which seems more likely to be present is not to be found in a thing, then that which seems [less] likely to be present will also not be in that thing. In weak mixtures, it appears that art could more easily match nature, and yet it cannot. Therefore <note>original: "Ergò"</note>, this can happen even less in stronger mixtures. The major premise is proven from the **logical argument of the greater** <note>original: "Argumento Topico à Majore"; a classical rhetorical rule stating that if a more likely premise is false, the less likely one must also be false</note>. The minor premise is evident to the external senses, because we judge the strong or weak mixture of a thing by its easy or difficult generation and decay; thus a horse, a fish, and all living animals can easily decay, and therefore they are of a weak mixture;

Gold and silver, however, do not decay so very easily; therefore, they consist of a strong composition. Since, therefore, art cannot match the power of nature in the generation of a horse or a fish, this is even less possible in the generation of those things which consist of a strong composition, such as gold and silver. ## The eighth objection.

Likewise, it is impossible for one **species** <term>Species: a distinct category or kind of substance</term> to be transformed into another. Metals are distinct according to their specific properties. **Therefore** <note>original: "Ergo"</note>. The **major premise** <term>Major: the primary statement of a logical argument</term> is clear according to the statement of the **Philosopher** <note>original: "Philosophi"; referring to Aristotle, the ultimate authority for medieval and early modern scholars</note> in Book 4 of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "Meteororum"</note>. The **minor premise** <term>Minor: the secondary statement of a logical argument</term> is likewise quite clear; for because they do not have the same properties and effects, they consequently do not have the same forms. They are only the same according to their **general concept** <term>General-Concept: a broad classification</term>, which is that they are metals, just as a human and a horse agree in that they are living things; but according to their particular **special properties** <term>Special-Eigenschafften: the unique characteristics that define a specific type</term>, one is distinct from the other. Just as no horse can be made from a human, and conversely no human from a horse, so also no other metal can be manufactured from a specific metal. This argument and its resolution are also put forward by Geber.

## The ninth objection.

Likewise, whoever does not know those **principles** <term>Principia: the fundamental origins or natural laws</term> that contribute to the generation and introduction of a certain form into a mixed being is not capable of manufacturing such a mixed being. **Alchemists** are of this kind. **Therefore** <note>original: "Ergo"</note>. The major premise is clear, because those principles that contribute to the generation and introduction of a certain form are the stars and heavenly bodies with their motion and light, as the Philosopher maintains in his books *On the Heavens and the World* <note>original: "de cœlo & mundo"</note>, and likewise *On the Causes of the Properties of the Elements* <note>original: "de causis proprietatum elementorum"</note>; for they are those things which—concerning what has been undertaken by sensible creatures—initially [perform] the nature of **generation** <term>Generation: the act of coming into being</term> and **corruption** <term>Corruption: the act of decaying or ceasing to be</term>...

### The tenth objection.

Likewise, just as art relates to nature, so do the methods of art relate to natural effects. However, art and nature are not the same thing, nor can they be: therefore, the methods of art and natural effects cannot be the same, and consequently, gold produced by art and natural gold are not the same. The **minor premise** is to be proven because nature produces a composite being in an instant, whereas art does so gradually; also, nature presupposes a matter, but art makes it, as is said in the **second book of the *Physics*** <note>original: "libro secundo physicorum"; a foundational work by Aristotle on the principles of nature</note>. Likewise, because every work produced by art is a desired and voluntary work, just as it is chosen and craved, as is evident from the **second book of the *Metaphysics*** <note>original: "libro secundo Metaphysicæ"; another key Aristotelian text</note>, nevertheless, that same work is changed in many ways according to the will of the artist; nature, however, always proceeds in an orderly fashion and in the same way. Thus, gold produced by art and natural gold are not the same.

### The twelfth objection.

Similarly, this is also known from experience; for the ancient **philosophers** <note>In this context, "philosophers" refers to natural scientists and alchemists of antiquity</note> have the custom of explaining the sciences to their students and other descendants both in writing and by word of mouth without ill-will. However, one finds that none of the ancient philosophers have done so in this art. Therefore, it appears that they knew nothing of this art, and consequently, that it is not possible. For we see in other sciences that every one of the ancient philosophers endeavored to sincerely present that which he knew in a **discipline** <note>A branch of knowledge or field of study</note>, because their desire was that others might become their equals in science. Therefore, the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle was often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and early modern texts</note> says in the **first book of the Metaphysics** <note>original: "primo Metaphysicæ"</note>, that it is a sign of a person who understands a matter that he is able to teach it. Since we therefore find recorded regarding this matter only old and **worthless scraps** <note>original: "Scartequen"; referring to discarded or low-quality manuscripts and pamphlets</note>, poetic fables serving no purpose, several laughable and fictional things, and words wandering far from the subject—in which nothing but pure lies and errors are to be found, as is clearly seen in the **operation** <term>Operation: the practical laboratory process of alchemy</term>—it is sufficient to conclude from this that this is no true art. Indeed, what is even worse, their successors still increase such errors daily and expand them beyond all number. This objection is touched upon twice by **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note> and answered by him.

### The fourteenth objection.

Likewise, they conclude even more strongly from that which is granted by them / for they say / that there is a single **stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold.</note> in this art / which becomes white and red / according as they wish only to prepare it / and which hardens the soft metals / namely by transforming **Saturn** <term>Saturnum: Alchemical code for lead.</term> and **Jupiter** <term>Jovem: Alchemical code for tin.</term> into gold and silver / on the other hand, it softens the hard metals / in that it transforms ore and iron into gold and silver / and makes mercury curdled <note>Meaning to solidify or "fix" the liquid mercury.</note> / so that it can be transformed into gold and silver. This stone is a single stone. *Therefore.* [Ergo] The **Major** <term>Major premise: the first statement in a logical syllogism.</term> is clear from this / because every thing in and of itself has only a single form and perfection / so also in and of itself there must likewise be only a single effect / which proceeds from such a form / as is evident from the **second book of On Generation and Corruption.** <note>original: "de generatione & corruptione"; a scientific work by Aristotle regarding how things are created and decay.</note> But if there are two contrary effects / which proceed from one form / then one of those effects must necessarily proceed from that same form in and of itself and **primarily** <note>original: "primario"</note> / but the other in an accidental way and **secondarily** <note>original: "secundario"</note> / because it is indeed impossible / that two things entirely opposed to one another be found in one thing at the same time. No less are metals, after they have been melted, of the same nature as mercury; and just as stones float upon mercury, they likewise float upon molten metals and do not sink. Molten glass alone gives way to stones and lets them sink because of its own and also foreign viscous stickiness (<term>viscosity<gloss>original: "viscositatem."</gloss></term>). Nevertheless, there is nothing liquid besides metals that possesses this moisture, except glass that has been placed in the fire and melted, due to its actual great viscosity; but once it has cooled, it no longer possesses such moisture, having been actually deprived of it. For in a metal that has cooled or is in the fire, there is a far greater viscosity than in molten ones. ### The Sixteenth Objection.

Likewise, they <note>The alchemists.</note> seem to claim that they do not create metals anew, but rather that they only make those metals perfect which are imperfect, by saying that only gold and silver are perfect metals, while the others are imperfect. We, on the contrary, say that this cannot be, because every matter that has its essence in a constant natural thing is perfect as far as its natural form is concerned. However, the matter of tin, lead, <term>copper<gloss>original: "Ertz." The <term>major premise<gloss>original: "Major." ## The Seventeenth Objection.

Likewise, those things which are increased by Nature in their kind through generation <note>The process of being born, created, or reproduced.</note> and preservation are perfect as far as their essential form is concerned; those metals which are called "imperfect" are of this kind just as much as gold and silver. <term>Therefore, etc.<gloss>original Latin: "Ergò &c." The <term>Minor</term> is known to the external senses; therefore, these metals cannot be called "imperfect" and others "perfect," but rather it is better to call these noble and those base. The base metals, however, cannot be transformed into noble ones in the way they claim. For we do not see a goat transformed into a horse, nor a horse into a human being, as something more noble. Consequently, such base metals will by no means be transformed into nobler ones in the manner they describe. Thus, these metals cannot be transformed into those others for the reason they give—that some are imperfect and others perfect. Look at the <term>Resolution<gloss>original Latin: "Resolution." ## The eighteenth Objection.

<margin>Perhaps better manufactured.</margin>
Likewise, those things which are brought into order by a final arrangement leading to a single result cannot have one and the same essential and proper form. <term>Alchemical Gold<gloss>Gold produced through laboratory processes rather than mined from the earth.</gloss></term> and <term>Silver</term> are not produced through a final arrangement leading to the same result as natural gold and silver. Therefore, etc. The <term>Major premise<gloss>The first part of a logical argument (syllogism) that states a general rule.</gloss></term> is proven because the essential and proper form is that which, arriving at the matter last, completes and perfects the thing through the final arrangement. Accordingly, where the final arrangement is not the same, the same essential and proper form will not be found, and consequently, it will not be the same <term>Species<gloss>The specific category or "kind" of a substance that defines its nature.</gloss></term>. The <term>Minor premise<gloss>The second part of a logical argument that provides specific evidence for the case at hand.</gloss></term> is self-evidently clear, because an <term>Alchemist</term> casts the metals by fire and adds his external aids to them, which are intended to give them the right and proper form; however, nature does not do this.

## The nineteenth Objection.

Likewise, those things whose modes of generation <note>The process by which something is born or created.</note> are not the same are not the same in themselves; and those things which are generated in the same way are the same themselves, as the <term>Philosopher<gloss>A standard title for Aristotle in academic and alchemical texts.</gloss></term> says in the <note>original: "Lib. 7. topicorum"</note> seventh book of the *Topics*. However, the generation of gold and silver by nature and by art does not happen in the same way. Therefore, the generated things themselves will not be the same. A similar argument can be drawn from <term>Corruption<gloss>In natural philosophy, the process of a substance breaking down or losing its form; the opposite of "generation."</gloss></term>. For this reason, <term>Alchemy</term> is not a true art, but only an imaginary one. The Major and Minor premises are clear in themselves.

Likewise, one can have no truth nor grounded knowledge of such things that arise only through mere chance. <term>Alchemy</term> is of this kind. ### The fifth objection of Aristotle and the twenty-sixth in order.

The fifth objection is taken from <term>prime matter<note>original: "erste Materie"; in Aristotelian philosophy, this is the fundamental, formless "stuff" that underlies all physical things before they take a specific shape or "form."</note></term>, by means of which all <term>generation<note>Coming into being.</note></term>, <term>corruption<note>The process of a thing ceasing to exist as itself; decay or dissolution.</note></term>, and transformation from one <term>species<note>A specific type of substance, such as lead or gold.</note></term> into another occurs; and it is formulated thus: Everything that is transformed from one species into another must be <term>resolved<note>original: "resolviret"; broken down or dissolved into its most basic, undifferentiated components.</note></term> into its prime matter—that is, matter which is stripped of its <term>first form<note>The internal "blueprint" or essence that makes a substance what it is.</note></term>—so that the form to which it was destined can be brought into it. The alchemists do not do it this way. <term>Therefore, etc.<note>original: "Ergò &c."; a shorthand indicating the conclusion of a logical syllogism.</note></term> The <term>major premise<note>original: "Major"; the primary general statement in a logical argument.</note></term> is clear, because through the resolution of a thing into its prime matter, generation and corruption arise, and not otherwise, because such a movement is toward the <term>essential form<note>The core identity of a substance.</note></term>; and this movement, which brings a thing to its essential form, is actually the transformation, and not merely a movement <note>meaning a change in quality rather than a change in essence</note>, as is proven in the <note>original: "quinto physicorum"; referring to the fifth book of Aristotle’s *Physics*, a foundational text for medieval science.</note> **fifth [book] of the Physics**. In change, increase, and decrease, there is actually a movement [of accidents], as is said there. Therefore, generation is accomplished when that which was not there before finds itself present, which behaves in the same way as <term>decaying<note>original: "Verwesung"; used here as a synonym for "corruption," the opposite of generation.</note></term>, and both are diametrically opposed to each other. The remaining movements happen from one thing into another, and in a somewhat contrary opposition. The <term>minor premise<note>original: "Minor"</note></term> is obviously clear. For they do not resolve the metals into their prime matter; therefore, they neither generate such nor do they annihilate them, but only change them into something else; for they melt the metal in the fire, and after it has been melted in such a way, they cast in some of their <term>juices<note>original: "Säfften"; often referring to chemical solutions, tinctures, or "elixirs" used in the alchemical process.</note></term>, which they first prepared through <term>alchemy<note>original: "Alchymie"</note></term>, which changes it so that it becomes similar to gold or silver. For through melting alone it is not resolved into prime matter, but some external and imaginary things are added to it; therefore, because they do not first [strip] the metal of its first form...

# Proofs for the Art.

...will become; but because the aforementioned points seem to be enough for now, we shall pass over them in silence.

## Here follow the Proofs that confirm the truth of the Art of making Gold.

That the aforementioned Art of making gold is founded in truth is proven in three ways. First, from proven authors who have written about it; second, with strong reasoning; and third, with analogies and clear examples. Since every sensible person who uses their reason correctly considers that the testimony of the wise in their arts and sciences is a strong ground of proof for bringing hidden and difficult truths to light. Therefore, it is said in <term>Dialectics</term> <note>original: "Dialecticis"; the formal study of logical argument and reasoning used by scholars to reach the truth.</note>: "One must give credit to every expert in his own art." And Aristotle says in <term>the tenth book of Ethics</term> <note>original: "libro decimo ethicorum"; referring to Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*, a foundational text for medieval and early modern philosophy.</note>: "It certainly appears that the opinions of the wise are worth as much as strong proofs." Thus, the truth of this Art is indeed demonstrated by many authors; hence we find that the most famous and ancient philosophers, who wrote much about other arts and sciences and endeavored to clearly bring their truth to light, confess that they also composed books on this Art. They teach that this Art is very strongly founded in truth and most diligently imitates nature; it also regulates nature within its own matter toward its <term>intended</term> <note>original: "intendirten"; referring to the "teleological" belief that nature has a specific goal or "end" for every substance, such as lead eventually "wanting" to become gold over eons.</note> purpose—which nature itself could never reach—and does so in only one way, as shall be described. # Proofs for the Art.

After the author initially proved such an Art from the most reliable authors, he now proves it with reasons, and primarily with two.

Secondly, it is further proven with reasons—and primarily with two—although it is difficult to confirm such an Art with reasons. Therefore the Philosopher <note>The "Philosopher" is the standard title used in this period to refer to Aristotle (384–322 BCE).</note> says in the first book of the *Topics* <note>original: "primo topicorum"; one of Aristotle's works on the art of dialectic and reasoning.</note>: There are certain problems <note>original: "Problemata"</note> about which one has conflicting arguments that appear plausible on both sides, yet they carry a doubt with them as to whether the matter actually is as it seems or not, because of the probable reasons on both sides. And there are also certain problems for which one can provide no proof because of their difficulty, etc. And among these is also the Art of making gold. I only say that, just as in the other sciences that aim at an operation <note>An "operation" refers to practical, manual, or experimental work (like medicine or chemistry) rather than purely theoretical study.</note>, it is proven that they are indeed true, so it will also be sufficient in this science, since it belongs among them. Therefore the Philosopher also says in the first and third books of the *Topics*, when he employs this hypothesis: If we have proven that it is so with other things, then we have also sufficiently demonstrated the truth of the matter at hand. Just as, therefore, when we wish to prove the truth of a thing perceived by the senses in those sciences which have an operation as their final goal, we prove it solely through a demonstration perceived by the senses, by showing how the basis of such proof must be taken from the senses and not from the intellect; in the same way, we must also proceed in this Art. ### Proof-Arguments for the Art.

...must be shown through the external senses. The same is also true in geometry, astronomy, music, optics, and the other sciences whose end-goal results in practice and operation. The <term>minor premise</term> <note>original: *Minor*; the second part of a logical argument.</note> cannot be proven except through **experiments** <note>original: *Experimenta*</note>. With this agrees what **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire.</note> says in the third book *On Crises* <note>original: *de crisi*</note>, namely:

> that the investigation of truth in every art and its confirmation is taken from its effects and their discovery. And how the same is derived from its **first principles** <note>original: *Principiis*</note>, etc.

From which it then becomes clear that these and almost all other arts cannot be proven from their theoretical **principles** <note>original: *Principiis*</note>, but rather from their **operations** <note>original: *Operationibus*; the practical results and works.</note>. Therefore **Avicenna** says in his treatise:

> Experience, however, bears witness that one can and should believe in the art itself.

### Proof-Arguments for the Art.

And this is not difficult in metals / because they are not distinct beings from one another / but are entirely of the same essence. 

The **minor premise** <term>Minor; the second step in a logical syllogism</term> thus becomes clear / because anyone who wishes to recognize gold and silver according to their true form / must recognize them through their **properties** <term>Eigenschafften</term>, **passions** <term>Passiones; the qualities a substance undergoes or its reactive behaviors</term>, and effects / whether they consist of action or of suffering <note>In this philosophical context, "suffering" refers to how a material is acted upon, such as being melted by fire or flattened by a tool.</note>.

In whatever metal that has been transformed through **alchemy** <term>Alchymie</term> / we accordingly encounter all **properties**, **accidents**, and effects of gold / from that we must necessarily conclude / that it is true gold / and if even one of these conditions which we have named is missing / then it is not true gold. Since therefore **chemical** <term>Chymische</term> gold has all the aforementioned **properties** in itself / we necessarily conclude from this / that it is true gold. 

Experience, however / as has been said / bears witness here / according to the decree of the wise and according to the external senses. But if it is not the very same gold as that which is dug from the earth / then they <note>those who deny alchemy</note> must necessarily assume / that these same **properties** all originate from contrary forms / which is completely impossible : therefore they must be of the same kind.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and scientific justification for alchemy, specifically using the theory of "spontaneous generation." The author argues that because some plants and animals can be produced both by seeds and by rotting (putrefaction), the "Art" of alchemy can likewise produce genuine minerals and metals that are identical to those formed by nature.</meta>

->### **Arguments for the Proof of the Art.**<-

Nature generates from <term>putrefaction <note>The process of decay or rotting which, in pre-modern science, was believed to spontaneously generate new life.</note></term> purslane, cabbage, stalks, pellitory, pumpkins, and many other types of plants. And these same plants also arise from their own seeds; they possess the same blossoms, leaves, and seeds, and are thus preserved and propagated in their own kind through the same seeds. This is also explained by **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> in the first book of *On the Properties of Foodstuffs* <note>original: *in primo alimentorum*</note>, in the chapter on fennel, where he says: "And this is something spontaneous, because it is generated just like anise, yet they are also sown in gardens." Therefore we say that there are some things which are generated solely through natural propagation, such as humans, otters, whales, and the palm tree. Others, however, are generated only through putrefaction, such as lice, fleas, grass, earthworms, and other imperfect things. Still others are generated in both ways, such as mice and purslane, etc.

# The Difficulties of the Art

## The First Cause of the Difficulty

Because this operation does not proceed by the course of nature alone; but rather, if one wishes to confess the plain truth, Art itself—and its investigation and the power of its effect together with its fulfillment—far surpasses nature and behaves as a miracle. This is because the final goal of this Art is certainly considered equal to those Divine works that surpass nature, just as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of the alchemical tradition</note> has said. Therefore Barseus, in the book which is called the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "turba Philosophorum"; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting of Greek philosophers</note>, reveals a great difficulty in his words, indicating that its power is very great because it can be recognized by no other foundation than through Divine inspiration, etc. For it is the greatest treasure and gift of God. 

And Rosinus <note>likely Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist often cited in later texts</note> says: Those devoted to the Art can in no way separate the truth from those things that the Philosophers have stated as doubtful, except only through Divine inspiration or the instruction of a person. Rasis <note>the Latinized name for Al-Razi, a Persian physician and alchemist</note> in *The Light of Lights* <note>original: "lumine luminum"</note> says: From this you should therefore consider to what extent Divine goodness has wished to reveal such things. 

And Hermes says: Understanding and reason perceive nothing else than how one should drive away the rust <note>rust: in an alchemical context, this refers to the impurities or "leprosy" of imperfect metals that must be removed to reach their pure core</note>. And Senior <note>the Latinized name for the 10th-century Arab alchemist Ibn Umail</note> says: They have kept nothing hidden except only the preparation, because it is the most difficult among all things; therefore, even when they have found a substance, they have lacked the preparation, and no thing is completed unless it happens through the preparation. 

And Mundus says: Some have erred for the reason that they did not know how to handle the matter. And Morienus says: Whoever applies himself to this Art must know the other disciplines well, and especially **logic** <term>Dialectic: the art of reasoning and debating; here it refers to the skill of deciphering the logical puzzles and metaphors used in alchemical texts</term>, because the wise ones of this Art have spoken only in flowery and dark words. 

And Theophilus in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* says: No one knows what the Philosophers have recorded in their books without diligent reading, testing, and investigation of the opinions of the wise; for what they have established is higher and more hidden than can be easily understood. ...cited passages: Whoever bends his back to read our books and diligently lies over them, not entangling himself in vain thoughts, and prays to GOD, he will rule in an imperishable kingdom as long as he lives. And Rosinus <note>Likely Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist whose name was often Latinized as Rosinus in medieval texts</note> says: Those who apply themselves to this Art, but have no understanding or knowledge <term>knowledge (Wissenschafft); here referring to systematic philosophical study</term> of those things that the Philosophers have described in their books, they err in many ways, etc. Thus, its nature, treatment, understanding, diligence, and governance indicate the greatest difficulty and obscurity in this Art.

### The Second Cause of the Difficulty.

Likewise, one can conclude its difficulty from the differences among those who are engaged in it today; for we see that they perform the operation <term>operation; the physical and chemical process of the alchemical work</term> today in many and various ways, and with different and foreign materials, and in both ways, error is attributed to the Art. Therefore Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher whose works were foundational to medieval medicine</note> says at the beginning of his *Commentary on the Regimen of Acute Diseases* <note>original: "Commentario regiminis acutorum"; a commentary on a work by Hippocrates</note>: From the differences found among those who cultivate <note>original: "excoliren"; to practice or refine through study</note> an art—regardless of which art it may be—man necessarily doubts. So that which has made him doubtful does not stem from the science <term>science (Wissenschafft)</term>, but from error; however, their uniform opinion in the same is a great confirmation of the science.

### The Third Cause of the Difficulty.

In the same way, one can conclude the difficulty by considering its rarity, because very seldom is someone found who has obtained it through experience itself. Therefore the Philosopher <note>Usually a reference to Aristotle, the "Philosopher" of the medieval and Renaissance schools</note> says in the *Sixth Book of Topics* <note>original: "sexto topicorum"; part of Aristotle's works on logic and dialectic</note>: Everything that is unusual is obscure, etc.

No less can one also conclude such difficulty in regard to the words with which everyone seems to contradict himself, and other things. So that therefore not everyone...

### The Fifth Cause of the Difficulty.

Likewise, a great difficulty in this art is concluded regarding its value, because they sometimes say that this stone is of no or very little value—as Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and foundational figure in alchemy</note>, Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught the secrets of the Stone to the King of Egypt</note>, and Haly <note>Likely Haly Abenragel or Khalid ibn Yazid, influential figures in the transmission of Arabic science to the West</note> say—and that it is found on the road and in the muck. At other times, however, they say that a person cannot reach the perfection of this art without great expense, and that nature is very precious and dear. Therefore, Zeno <note>A speaker appearing in the "Turba Philosophorum"</note> says in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "turba Philosophorum"; one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between ancient sages</note>: The stone you seek is publicly sold for a low price. And Barseus says in the quoted place: For what you seek is not of little value. And Zeno: Again, the philosophers have also caused the common folk <note>original: "Pöbel"; the uneducated or uninitiated masses</note> to err greatly in this art by saying that the nature of the stone is lowly, as it is sold for a paltry thing. And by saying, on the other hand, that the nature of this stone is more precious than all other natures, they have deceived the ignorant in their books. Thus, you should know that the art requires two natures; for nothing precious is made without something lowly, nor anything lowly without something precious, etc. And Daucus: Do not ponder anything else in this art, and especially in the preparation of gold.

From what has been said so far, and what is still to be said, it is clear that all names of this stone are invented for the purpose of ensuring that those who do not seek it rightly will go astray. ->### The Difficulties of the Art.<-
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

...flowery, dark, allegorical, and ambiguous ways of speaking that occur therein. For it [the Art] has been presented entirely in the aforementioned manner, as clearly appears from the books of the Philosophers <note>original: "Philosophorum"</note>. And that a difficulty is to be found in such teachings, the Philosopher <note>original: "Philosophus"; likely referring to Aristotle, often called "The Philosopher" in medieval and early modern texts</note> indicates in the sixth book of the *Topics* <note>original: "sexto topicorum"; a work by Aristotle on the art of dialectic and logic</note>, where he says:

> For it happens that in such allegorical ways of speaking, the truth is misrepresented <note>original: "verlästert"; literally slandered or blasphemed, here meaning the truth is obscured or treated with indignity through poor metaphor</note>.

And in the 8th book of the *Topics* <note>original: "topicorum"</note>, he says that a presentation is difficult to prove because it uses obscure names—whether they are spoken in a simple or complex way—or because the matter cannot be known if the described thing is only spoken of in general or allegorical terms, etc. Indeed, what is even more difficult and obscure is that the Art has been presented with unusual words, which teaching style is even worse than the allegorical one, as he argues in the sixth book. Therefore, it is said there:

> There are some things which are taught neither in an allegorical manner nor with ambiguous words, and these are even worse than allegories; just as the law is a measure or image of what is naturally just <note>original: "billig"; in this context, it refers to equity and natural justice rather than "cheapness"</note>.

And for this reason, they are worse than allegories: because an allegory makes a thing known through the similarity of what is said, whereas unusual ways of speaking do not. Therefore, the investigation of these terms—and consequently their effect—is quite difficult. Indeed, when the authors wish to demonstrate something, they explain one unknown thing by another equally unknown or perhaps even more unknown thing; this method of explaining and understanding is the very worst, as appears from the cited passage.

Therefore, one should not wonder if the students of the art <term>students of the art (Kunstgeflissene); those dedicated to the study of alchemical theory and philosophy</term> and laboratory workers <term>laboratory workers (Laboranten); practitioners who perform physical experiments in the workshop or lab</term> err greatly in this science. They cannot confirm with proof that this or that intention of the wise ones <term>intention of the wise ones (Intention der Weisen); the hidden meaning or specific objective intended by the alchemical masters</term> is certain and settled until they actually possess this art in practice or are close to achieving it. Thus, it seems to me that obtaining the Art is almost impossible, whether through oral instruction or through divine inspiration, even if one well and truly recognizes the explanation of many figurative speeches.

## The Seventh Cause of the Difficulty.

Likewise, many difficulties arise for this Art regarding the way and manner in which it is presented and treated. This is because all other arts and sciences proceed rhetorically <note>original: "rhetorice"</note>—except for this one. Every other art explains its principles <note>original: "Principia"</note> and technical terms <note>original: "Terminos"</note> in orderly chapters, along with descriptions and explanations of names, as well as the instruments <note>original: "Instrumenta"</note> through which one attains the knowledge and science of their conclusions and their work (wherein the final goal is found). Every other art strives to demonstrate and prove everything as clearly as possible, according to the utmost ability of every person.

This Art alone, however, does the opposite. It undertakes to teach what it is and what its function consists of without first providing knowledge of its principles, terms, and instruments. It mixes in now this, now that; it presents things partly diminished and partly in excess; and it does so both without order and in a reversed order. It begins with its final goal without explaining that goal, and it strives to present everything obscurely and to hide it as much as it possibly can. Therefore, Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher; in alchemy, he is often cited as a founding authority on the nature of matter</note> says in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "turba Philosophorum"; a famous medieval alchemical text where ancient philosophers debate the secrets of the Art</note>: "You should know that the envious ones <note>The "envious" or *invidiosi* are the masters who intentionally hid secrets to keep them from the unworthy</note> in this work have related the completion sooner than the beginning." And Rosinus <note>An Arabic corruption of the name Zosimos of Panopolis, a major early alchemist</note> says: "You should know that the philosophers <note>original: "Philosophi"</note> have presented nothing but hidden and dark things in the beginning, middle, and end of their works. Therefore they have never ceased to conceal, etc."

## The Eighth Cause of the Difficulty.

Likewise, it seems to us that there is no small difficulty regarding the vessel in which the cooking <note>In alchemy, "cooking" or digestion refers to the steady application of heat to the matter</note> is performed. For although they teach the making of various vessels for various effects they perform, there is nonetheless only one single vessel in which all functions occur during a decoction <note>original: "Decoction"; the process of boiling or extraction via heat</note>. This vessel is indeed only one—both regarding its matter <note>original: "Materie"</note> and its shape <note>original: "Figur"</note>, as well as its number—just as can be seen in the reproductive vessels <note>likely referring to the womb</note> of perfect living things.
