->### The Difficulties of the Art.<-

To transform silver into gold, certain weights and goals are determined, which anyone who wishes to produce such a thing should diligently strive to know. For if he knows these weights, he will understand the entire work; and whoever does not know such weights should not trouble himself with our books. For the <term>philosophers</term> <note>In this context, "philosophers" refers to alchemists and natural scientists of the medieval and Renaissance periods.</note> have not only set down nothing clear concerning this matter, but have hidden it most of all. And therefore the <term>Philosopher</term> <note>A standard reference to Aristotle, the ultimate authority on natural physics in this era.</note> in the fourth book of the *Physics* <note>original: "4. physicorum"</note> and the second book of *On the Heavens and the World* <note>original: "2. cœli & mundi"</note> maintains that for every natural action a certain time is determined, in which—and in no less or more—such a work reaches perfection. And <term>Galen</term> <note>An ancient Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> says in the second book of *On Critical Days* <note>original: "de diebus criticis"</note> that the movements and works of nature always observe a course and an order. 

However, the wise philosophers have harmoniously changed this time in their writings to lead the ignorant into error. Thus, some set this limit at one year, such as <term>Rosinus</term> <note>Likely Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist.</note> and <term>Plato</term> in his *Stollicis* <note>Likely referring to a pseudo-Platonic alchemical text.</note>: "And you should know that the few days of this preparation consist in the revolution of the greater light (the Sun)." <term>Rasis</term> <note>The Persian polymath Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi.</note>, however, sets it at nine months in the *Book of Three Words* <note>original: "libro trium verborum"</note>. Some set it at 7, others at 40, others at 80 days; others in countless other ways. Yet in truth, there is no more than one limit, because there is only one <term>decoction</term> <note>The process of heating or "cooking" the alchemical matter to mature it.</note> from the beginning to the end, as is evident from the generation of a child or a young chick. During this time, however, the secret of the fire must be enclosed, which is the most important thing in this art.

To recognize this day of judgment—both of the birth and the conception of the <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note>—which is the goal of the completion of the entire work, one must first know the day that indicates it. This is because the indicating day acts as the sign, and the indicated day acts as the thing signified, and they have a certain orderly natural connection to one another. For just as can be seen in the case of <term>putrid fevers</term> <note>original: "Febribus putridis"; a medical term for fevers caused by the corruption of bodily humors.</note>, in which the physician must know the days of indication and also the alternating days indicated by them, so that he may cure the sick person well—

## The Tenth Cause of Difficulty.

Furthermore, this art seems to be difficult in regard to the <term>matter</term> <note>original: "Materie," the raw base substance.</note> from which this Stone arises. For they use flowery speech so that they may lead the stubborn and ignorant astray. They name all things in the world / claiming that from them, according to different types of effects, the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>original: "Stein der Weisen"</note> can be made. Thus some have sought their intention and work in <term>arsenic</term> <note>original: "Arsenico"</note>, others in <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: "Schwefel"</note> / others in <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "Quecksilber"</note> / others in blood / others in eggs / others in hair / others in dung, etc., and so on in countless more things. And even regarding a single substance, there are completely different opinions / and they also operate in different ways / both with one thing alone / and also through the addition of others.

This refers to a logical demonstration where a single principle explains many specific instances.</note> that one thing is in many and from many, as is said in the cited place; but on the other hand, it is of the essence of the *particular proof* <note>original: "particular-Beweis"</note> that many things exist; therefore, that which is universal is one thing and more recognizable, and vice versa. Therefore, unity is the cause of multiplicity and its recognition, and not the other way around.

### An Objection Against the Said Unity.

However, it seems that there are many ways to this goal, and not just one alone. For <term>Geber</term> <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the "Father of Chemistry," whose Latinized works were central to Western alchemy.</note> says in the chapter *On the Nature of Sulfur* <note>original: "de natura sulphuris"</note>: Whoever also knows how to mix that same substance—namely, sulfur—during preparation and unite it with the <term>bodies</term> <note>original: "Cörpern" (corpora); in alchemy, this refers to the solid metals, while "spirits" are volatile substances.</note>, he will know one of the greatest secrets and the path to perfection, because there are many ways to one effect and one intention, etc. And <term>Rasis</term> <note>Rhazes (865–925 AD), a Persian polymath who categorized chemical substances and processes.</note> says in the *Book of the Perfect Mastery* <note>original: "libro perfecti magisterii"</note>, where he speaks of the bodies and <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "Spiritibus"; substances like mercury, sulfur, or arsenic that "flee" the fire.</note>, of their purification, and of their many and manifold couplings—which he spoke of previously—and of the different ways: I say finally, however, that each of the aforementioned bodies and spirits, when it has been prepared through a perfect preparation, whether it be white or red, is in itself alone the <term>Elixir</term> <note>The final medicinal or transformative substance sought by alchemists.</note>, etc. *Therefore* <note>original: "Ergo"</note> there can be more paths to perfection and more materials in this Art.

We answer, just as before, that there is only one way and only one matter; this was sufficiently clear when we dealt with the Unity of Matter, and it will be further clarified below. Regarding what Rasis says, however, we give this answer: that in the <term>Subject</term> <note>original: "Subjecto"; the underlying substance being operated upon.</note>, if one wishes to speak according to the true nature of the matter, the spirits and bodies are one and the same; they are only distinguished in terms of logical reasoning, as will be seen below. Therefore, that which is perfectly prepared, whether it be a body or a spirit, is in itself only one Elixir. Regarding the multiplicity of paths, however, we answer as was said before. the substance which provides nourishment truly nourishes; however, there are many *dispositions* <note>original: "Dispositiones"; here referring to the preparatory states or arrangements of matter required before the final transformation.</note> or paths that precede it, according to the variety of the preceding changes. These are almost innumerable when compared to the final goal itself. Yet, although these preparatory stages are many and distinct from one another, they are never altered in their orderly progression because of the final purpose they share. Therefore, in and of itself, there is only one path from the beginning to the end. Thus, there is only one single way to reach it. However, because preceding *dispositions* must necessarily exist before this final stage, many paths may be named; yet they possess a certain order and natural connection to that same single path which leads to the final goal. Therefore, they are never confused with one another, nor are they truly distinct. ### The first distinction, which shows that this art is both natural and divine, and that by means of it the ancient philosophers prophesied of future divine miracles.

Furthermore, this art compels us—as much because of its difficulty as its unusualness—to expand our discourse. We say that it is partly natural, and partly divine and above nature. For when it is considered insofar as the <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold.</note> is cast upon the imperfect metals—because it transforms them entirely into gold, just as nature does, whether one part is cast upon 100 or upon 1,000—then it is natural. And because secrets—especially these—are not to be revealed to everyone, but only to the worthy and those beloved by God, they have therefore written for those individuals alone. For if they had recorded this mystery for everyone without distinction, they would have revealed all the methods and circumstances by which one attains it with clear speech and order—as in all other sciences—without obscure talk and mysteries. Since, however, they wished to open such things only to the aforementioned [worthy] ones, but keep them hidden from the ignorant, they presented them with obscure—indeed, the very darkest—speech. # Why the Philosophers [Wrote] So Obscurely

...repeat [the process] yet again, where it is necessary, until you find that which you desire perfectly. And you must not allow yourself to be deterred from this matter by either the labor of your hands or the great expenses, because you will overcome through persistence and get through with patience, and through God's help, you will attain that which you have wished for, and thus carry away the reward for your labor and the profit from your great expenditure. Therefore, for the aforementioned reasons, the **Philosophers** <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to the "adepts" or master alchemists of antiquity and the Middle Ages.</note> have presented such an art in the manner just described.

Today, almost all together who strive only to make mere changes without actual transmutation <term>transmutation: the internal, essential change of a metal's nature, rather than just its outward appearance</term> (because they possess only weak and meager knowledge), can never reach this proper ultimate goal. They either believe that they can perform such things in many more ways and also with more things, or they change the metals in manifold ways—both in similar and in foreign substances—so that they look like gold and silver. And because this appears to no one as anything other than a deceitful work, all such people are rightly regarded as fraudsters. However, for this reason, the art itself cannot be called deceitful; such error is not to be found in the art itself, but is found in the artist who deviates from the grasp of such truth. For just as a thing behaves in its essence, so it also behaves in its knowledge, as it is said in the **Second [Book] of Metaphysics** <note>Original Latin: "secundo Metaphysicæ." A reference to Aristotle's work, which was a foundational text for medieval and early modern science.</note>. Therefore, because there is only a single essence of a thing, there will also be only a single knowledge of the same, and consequently, there must also be only one truth thereof. Those who thus depart from the unity and truth of the matter err in many—indeed, countless—ways: and so they believe, because of their ignorance and errors, that such an art is ruinous.

# ...written about this art.

Note here the operation and experience of Alchemy <note>The text uses the archaic spelling "Alchymie," referring to the ancient practice combining chemistry, philosophy, and mysticism.</note>, how it requires, as it were, a steady labor of the hands and visual observation at certain hours; namely, that one cleanses the elements and, after they have been cleansed, takes them into view and binds them together, etc.

Regarding what has been said so far, it should be noted that in this glorious art, the labor of the hands and visual observation are very necessary. The labor of the hands is necessary so that the superfluous part may be removed, which nature separates and cleanses throughout the entire duration of <term>Digestion: the process of softening or ripening a substance using steady, gentle heat</term> and <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to represent purification and "exaltation" of the matter</term> through the fire, in that one assists nature without a great interval. For although nature separates the superfluous on her own, she cannot immediately remove it unless she is helped; only the artist can do this. Therefore Socrates said: "Search for the coldness of the moon, and you shall find the heat of the sun, and let your hands labor diligently so that the burden may be lightened for you." And Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in chemistry and alchemy.</note> in his *Summa* <note>original: "Summa Perfectionis Magisterii," one of the most influential alchemical books of the Middle Ages.</note>: "And he who does not have his perfect limbs will not be able to reach the perfection of this work for himself, as if, for example, he is blind or injured in his external limbs, etc." For without hands, it is impossible for someone to attain this high wisdom. 

Thus, visual observation is indeed highly necessary, but especially at the end of the cooking and sublimation, so that an artist—after having removed everything superfluous—may behold a wonderful and shining white color, and immediately after such completion of the work, find rest. For when one then cools the Moon <note>In alchemical symbolism, the Moon represents silver and the "feminine," cool principle.</note>, the Sun <note>The Sun represents gold and the "masculine," hot principle.</note> becomes hidden in its innermost part, and the rising is united and bound with the setting, the Heaven with the Earth (according to the opinion of the ancient Sages), and the spiritual with the corporeal. # Why the Philosophers are so Obscure

...[Her]mes in the second <note>Likely referring to the second book of the *Septem Tractatus* or another work attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note>: For when coldness comes to that thing which is warm by nature, it will not harm it. And **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works were foundational to medieval alchemy.</note> says: You should know that if you have driven out all the vapor, then you have operated well in the **<term>Composition: the blending or combining of different substances into a single whole</term>**, but you have failed in the **<term>Calcination: the process of reducing a substance to a fine powder through intense heat</term>**; make the same cold, etc. For then the hidden becomes manifest, and the manifest becomes hidden, when it is cooled. And this cooling happens with a state of rest, in which rest no labor of the hands is found, because it is the end of the work. Of which **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist known for his dialogue with King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: This is that **<term>Disposition: the final state or arrangement of the alchemical matter</term>** which cannot be achieved with hands, etc.

And **Pythagoras** speaks in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, which presents a debate between various pre-Socratic philosophers.</note>: You should know that the thing of which the **Philosophers** have spoken in many ways reaches its companion without the fire, just as the magnet stone reaches the iron, and causes many colors to be found in the same, etc. It is as if he were saying that one no longer required the fire, but rather united the **<term>Spirits: the volatile, "soul-like" parts of a substance that can be vaporized</term>** and the bodies with the iron.

The first operation, which happens with the hands, is the first degree of the work, which occurs through **<term>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance into vapor so it purifies and resettles as a solid</term>** and cleansing. The other operation, however, which happens with rest and without any manual procedure, is the second degree of the work; it happens through the retention and persistence of that which has been sublimated and cleansed, because then the active agent, when it brings about the form, finishes the work, rests, and delights itself. For delight is to be found more in rest than in movement, according to the seventh book of the *Ethics* <note>original: "7. ethicorum," referring to Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note>.

From what has been proven so far, we can therefore conclude that no one can reach the goal and completion of this glorious, hidden art solely through diligence and a multitude of books; rather, he must possess a naturally deep and high understanding, so that he knows how to distinguish the figures and parables of true things in their many and varied necessary meanings. For the first figure of one and the same word will have one meaning in one place, and a contrary meaning in another, as **Rasis** <note>The Latinized name of Al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian physician and chemist.</note> says in *The Light of Lights* <note>original: "Lumine Luminum"</note>, where he speaks of the elements. ### The third Distinction, which shows that this Art is more certain than other sciences, and likewise noble, brief, and easy.

Furthermore, we say that this art is more certain than all others, because all **philosophers** <note>original: "Philosophi." Neither the opinions nor the words are different when considering the true nature of the matter, but only in appearance, due to the reasons mentioned above. Thus, the total agreement of them all shows that this art is more certain and more truthful than all others. For in all other arts and sciences, opinions are commonly divided concerning the subject in question, and are sometimes interpreted in different and contrary ways, both in theory and in practice. Likewise, the entire true and certain operation of this art—because it is only one single process—can be understood in one day, indeed even in one hour, by an intelligent person, without any further investigation

This likely refers to a specific pseudo-Platonic alchemical text or a corruption of a title in the alchemical corpus.</note>: And whoever has recognized our intention and our goal is already a **Philosopher** and enriched; and whoever has not understood our words still finds himself in the snares of nature. But this **candle** of a wise man is like a bright-shining light throughout his whole life; but the children of nature are tormented in a dark place where such a candle does not shine, because they know nothing at all of this art. And <term>Morienus</term> says once more: For all who do not understand this art are very wretched people and true beggars; for what they do, they do so that they may have an abundance of all things, which they cannot obtain without this art.

But because this art is one and unique, the **Philosophers** also wish to have only one thing, and in this they all understand each other. Because of this unity, the art is itself more certain than others, truthful, easy, and brief.

# Error of those who operate.

Know then, O you sons of the wise, that this stone is very precious, and cries out: "Protect me, and I will protect you also: Help me to my right, so that I may help you also, for my sun and my rays lie hidden within me," etc. And in the first book of this same *treatise* <note>original: *Tractats*</note> he says: You should know that the vulture, who is upon the mountain, calls out from the peak of the same, and says with a clear voice: "I am white, yellow, and red," etc. Therefore *Parmenides* advises us well in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>Latin: *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note>, where he says: After all the properties and natures of the stone are known, then lay your hand to this work; but if you do not know the true properties, do not approach the same, because you would have nothing but harm, misfortune, and sadness from it. If, therefore, the beginning is unchangeable and immutable, then everything that is of the essence of such a beginning will also be unchangeable and immutable. But if the beginning undergoes a change and transformation, then everything that is of the essence of such a beginning, and belongs essentially to the beginning, will also be changed and transformed. Therefore, when the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in Books 2 and 18 of *On the Animals* <note>Latin: *de animalibus*</note> wishes to show that the testicles <note>Latin: *testiculi*</note> are among the most noble parts of our body, he says that after the principle <note>Latin: *principium*; the starting point or fundamental source</note> has been slightly transformed, much of that which is found near the same principle tends to be transformed at the same time. And in the first book of the *Physics* <note>Latin: *primo Physicorum*</note> he says: If one once establishes something absurd <note>Latin: *absurdes*</note>, then more absurdities <note>Latin: *absurda*</note> will follow thereafter. Therefore, if the principle <note>Latin: *principium*</note> of alchemy is to be unchangeable and remain immutable, then that which belongs to such a principle will necessarily be immutable and unchangeable. But if the former is changed, the latter will also necessarily be transformed. And if an error is found in the same principle, then the same will necessarily be found at the end and in the entire work. # Refutation of the Objections.

...which this divine art performs, especially since it is a secret of all secrets of the great and sublime God, as the **philosophers** <note>Referring to alchemists or "natural philosophers"</note> of this art speak, just as **Aristotle** taught this secret to **Alexander** through parables, speaking to him through examples, dark speeches, and signs, fearing that such a divine secret might fall into the power of the unbelieving and the arrogant, whom God deems unworthy; or that he himself, **Aristotle**, might become a transgressor of divine grace and a betrayer of the divine secret and the hidden revelation. For this reason, **Aristotle** spoke to **Alexander** in parables in the *Letter of the Book of Secrets* <note>original: *epistola libri secretorum*; a reference to the *Secretum Secretorum*, a medieval text falsely attributed to Aristotle that contains occult and alchemical knowledge</note>.

Now that many **distinctions** <note>original: *Distinctiones*; formal logical categorizations used in academic writing</note> and explanations of the same have been set forth—which contribute not a little to a better clarification of the presented question—it remains for us to now refute the presented **objections** <note>original: *Einwürffe*</note> that are intended to support the opposing view, along with several incidental questions and other noteworthy matters relevant to this topic.

Since the **dispositions** <note>original: *Dispositiones*; the preparatory states or arrangements of a substance or the mind</note> precede the **habit** <note>original: *Habitu*; in Scholastic philosophy, a "habit" is a stable, perfected state of being or knowledge</note> and make it fit for both the intellectual and actual forms, we have therefore set forth many dispositions in advance. By virtue of these, a wise lover of these things may well believe and properly prepare his senses and understanding to grasp the **habits** and forms of which we have spoken until now. Therefore, in what follows, we wish to describe the manner and way of attaining the **habit** and the form, along with several other **dispositions** of the wise and of our own teaching. In doing so, we begin first with the refutation of the reasons cited at the beginning—namely, those of people who do not understand this glorious science and wish to ruin it.

The answer to the first five objections is clear from what has been said thus far and what is yet to be said. For even if we wish to follow Nature through **alchemy**—that is, in the Work itself, by making the very same gold from the **principles** <note>original: *principiis*; the fundamental components, usually Mercury and Sulfur, from which all metals were thought to be composed.</note> of metals as Nature herself makes—this cannot happen in the same manner and method as Nature's work. This is because, regarding the manner and method of the work, Art <note>In alchemical literature, "Art" (*Ars*) refers to human technology and intervention, as opposed to spontaneous natural processes.</note> creates its Stone from these same **principles**, by means of which it transforms all metals into gold.

If, however, Art intended to create metals from scratch, then Art would be compelled to follow Nature in the manner and method of the work as well, concerning both the quantity of the elements and also the **proportion**, mixture, heat, time, and place; in that case, Art would be impossible. One cannot have certain knowledge of such things, but only through mere conjecture—knowledge which is useful only to one devoted to theory, but not to a **practitioner** <note>original: *practico*; one who actually works at the furnace.</note>.

However, when we consider it regarding the serving art, then this work is artificial—not that art generates, corrupts, and brings things into certain forms, but because it serves nature, which performs all of this. For God has distinguished the perfection of things from one another in many ways; because in those things in which the composition occurring according to nature is weak, He places a greater and nobler perfection, namely that which is found according to the soul. In animate things, however, the opposite is found. And therefore, we cannot form a lion, a goat, or a human—not in regard to the mixture, because it is weak in them, but rather in regard to their noble **Form**, which cannot submit itself to our actions. Likewise, although we may know how to bring about the generation of some mineral, vegetative, and animate things—whether they be of strong or weak mixture—we do not know their actual forms at all. However, in the generation of **gold**, we recognize its actual form, which is separated from all perfecting matter, as well as the manner of its perfection and union, by following Nature. ## Resolution of the Tenth Objection.

To the tenth objection, we reply: because some forms are natural while others are artificial, and among the natural ones, some are **essential** <note>original: *wesentlich*; the core nature that makes a thing what it is</note>, they are all brought in by nature in an instant following the preceding **dispositions** <note>original: *Dispositionibus*; the preparatory states or arrangements of matter</note> that make them fit for it, regardless of whether some practice of art accompanies their preparation or not. And these are the essential forms, which are the **principle of operation** <note>original: *Principium der Operation*; the internal source of a thing's active power or behavior</note> in all things. The **logician** <note>original: *Dialecticus*; a scholar of logic and formal reasoning</note> calls these the "proper forms" or "distinctions" that constitute a certain **species** <note>original: *Speciem*; a specific category of being</note>, and through them, every thing has its essence. 

But some are accidental forms which, if they flow and originate directly from the essential forms, are brought in by nature in an instant alongside the specific forms, because they are, as it were, the proper **attributes** <note>original: *Passiones*; in a philosophical sense, the qualities or "sufferings" that naturally belong to a substance</note> of the things; and these are the forms by virtue of which every thing properly acts. However, if they do not originate directly from the essential forms, then they are introduced gradually over time, such as color, smell, taste, and a specific, determined shape that follows their essential form, some of which [can be seen...]

...be entirely unique to a whole species, such as the color of a peacock [or] the shape of an elephant; but some are common, such as the color of a horse, a hen, and the scent of violets. The **artificial forms**, however, are all collectively **accidental** <note>original: *zufällig*; in Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that does not change the essential nature of a thing, like its color or shape</note>, and are nothing other than the shapes of things that have been brought into them through art. These may have become so according to the will of the artist—such as the shape of a house, a ship, or money—or by chance, as can be seen in the shapes of broken stones. Some of these remain in their essence, such as the shape of a house, but some do not; or they consist merely in the potential to become something, as can be seen in the **art of singing and dancing** <note>these were considered "transient" forms that only exist while the act is being performed</note>. All of these are brought in gradually over time, as is clear from the **seventh book of the Metaphysics** <note>original: *septimo Metaphysicæ*; a reference to Aristotle’s work on the nature of existence</note>, wherefore the **Philosopher** <note>original: *Philosophus*; a standard title for Aristotle in early modern academic writing</note> stated there that **artificial things** are counted as **essence** <note>original: *Wesen*</note> in terms of their **matter** <note>original: *Materie*</note>, but are counted as **accidents** <note>original: *Accidentibus*</note> in terms of their **form**.

Because the generation of the **Philosopher’s Stone** <note>original: *Stein der Weisen*; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold</note> therefore originates from nature by means of a natural active thing—namely fire—along with its natural color, scent, and natural form (which are accidental forms that follow its determined essential form, yet with the assistance of art, which has used the proper natural matter for its purpose in artificial tools), its form must necessarily be **natural and essential**. This essential form is recognized through its natural, accidental, and proper forms, just like all other things in the world. And although the execution and the manner of such execution [of the work] come from the will [of the alchemist], the form, which is generated in an instant, is natural. Therefore, the form of this Stone cannot be called "artificial," as some foolish people imagine. In the same way, this is also to be understood regarding the **gold** generated by this Stone, whose form is brought into it in an instant—as we have seen—and not gradually; though the preceding **dispositions** <note>original: *Dispositiones*; the preparatory states or chemical changes that make the matter ready to receive the "form" of gold</note> are indeed brought in gradually.

In the explanation of the tenth objection and its resolution, it is furthermore to be noted that natural forms are named either as those where Nature alone prepares a **matter** <note>original: *Materie*</note> for itself and brings the form into it—as in a human, a palm tree, marble stone, <term>etc.</term>—or where Art prepares a **matter** beforehand (though not through the final and primary preparation) and hands it over, so that Nature then fully prepares it and makes it capable of its own accord until the very end, with the assistance of Art, and subsequently brings the form into it. This can be seen in the production of <term>Uzifur</term> <note>an alchemical term for cinnabar or red mercuric sulfide</note>, white lead, <term>theriac</term> <note>a famous medical concoction or "universal" antidote made of dozens of ingredients</note>, and all compound things. For that which prepares the **matter** for a form beforehand does not itself give the form; however, that which prepares and **disposes** the **matter** for itself does so, because that same acting cause **disposes** for the form and also provides the form. 

There are, however, some forms that are both natural and accidental, which come from Nature alone without Art, and also from Nature through the help of Art—such as health—because the acting **principle** <note>original: *Principium*; the internal source of movement or change</note> of all these is internal, which is Nature. The artificial forms, however, are simply called "accidental" <note>in Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property like shape or color that does not change the essential substance of the thing</note>; for their presentation, Nature only prepares a **matter** from afar, depending on whether it requires much or little for it. Nature, however, would never be able to bring a form into them, because the external **principle** is missing in this **operation**. But Art, being powerful, takes this **matter** from Nature, prepares it, promotes it to a closer **disposition**, and gradually brings the form into it, just as is the form of a house, a ship, or a ring. Therefore, the natural and essential forms of things are not changed in their kind, although some are accidental <note>original: *zufällig*; non-essential or variable qualities, such as color or size</note> in regard to different lands. Likewise, in artificial things, Art strictly retains one and the same **matter** and a natural form, but changes the artificial forms as it pleases. In natural things, however—both those that Art serves and those it does not—one and the same **matter** is not retained; rather, the **matter** is constantly changed so that it may be **disposed** toward a different form, according to the various qualities of the **matter**. Since the Philosopher's Stone is therefore generated by Nature through the help of Art and through Divine Power, which wishes to reveal it, the Stone itself, its form, and the alchemical gold cannot be called artificial, but must certainly be called natural. Art is also connected with Nature because Nature is the **principle** <note>original: *Principium*; the foundational source or starting point</note> of Art, as is clear from the **second [book] of the Physics** <note>original: *secundo physicorum*; referring to Aristotle’s *Physics*, Book II, which discusses nature as a source of change</note>—namely, insofar as it comes from its heavenly origin, whose **principle** is the **active intellect** <note>original: *würckende Verstand*; in Aristotelian philosophy, the aspect of the mind that makes thinking possible</note>. The **principle** of Nature, however, belongs to **speculation** <note>original: *Speculation*; here meaning philosophical contemplation or the theoretical study of divine and natural truths</note>, because the work of Nature is a work of **speculation**; indeed, Nature itself is a work and **instrument** <note>original: *Instrument*</note> of the same. Thus, it is clear to what extent this Art, as well as its works and its form, is natural, and to what extent it is not.

# Refutation of the Objections.

...the *form* is already attained, as when a knowledgeable person already begins to perform *meditations* <note>Reflective or analytical thoughts.</note> upon a matter. The first *potentiality* <note>original: "Potentia"; the capacity for a thing to become something else.</note> is threefold: namely, a near-related, a remote, and a most remote one. The near-related is so called because, once it is applied to an active cause and united with it, it assumes the actual essence or the *form* after even a slight change; as is stated in the *ninth book of the Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle's "Metaphysics," Book 9, which focuses on potentiality and actuality.</note> and the *second book of On the Heavens and the World* <note>original: "secundo cœli & mundi," referring to Aristotle's "De Caelo."</note>; just as nourishment finds itself in its final *disposition* <note>The final state or arrangement of matter before it changes.</note> toward that which can be nourished. The remote potentiality, however, is so called because it requires several more changes. But the most remote is that in which a certain *suitability* <note>original: "Convenienz"</note> is found between the thing that is being transformed and the thing into which it is being transformed—much like how the elements and the sprouting of grain-bearing plants relate to the nourishment of our own bodies. 

And regarding this remote and most remote *potentiality*, the *Philosopher* <note>A common historical title for Aristotle.</note> says in the *ninth book of the Metaphysics* that one cannot say of the earth, before it has been transformed into ore, that it exists in the *potentiality* for the *form* of a bronze pillar; nor can one say of trees, before they have been felled and carpentered, that they exist in the *potentiality* for the *form* of a house. The *potentiality* of the attained *form*, however, is called the *actuality* <note>original: "Actus"</note> itself, as is evident from the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de anima"</note>, and is twofold: namely, the first, as having knowledge of a thing; and the second, as performing *meditations* upon it. It is impossible to reach the second *actuality* unless the first is already present. 

Therefore, according to the order, there is first the most remote *potentiality*; second, the remote; third, the near-related; fourth, the first *actuality*, which is the *form*; and fifth, the second *actuality*, which is the *habit* <note>original: "Habitus," referring to a settled disposition or state of being.</note> that arises from the *form*. Regarding this *form*, it is said in the *second book of On the Soul* that the *actualities* exist before the *potentialities*. The same is also said in the *ninth book of the Metaphysics*. And *Aristotle* also said in the *second book of On the Heavens and the World*: 

> There is only one single perfect good, which requires no *operation* <note>In this context, an "operation" is an action or process required to achieve perfection; God or the "perfect good" is already complete.</note>

Furthermore, we say that the perfect and the imperfect are named in three ways in things: In the first way, in those that have the same form; in the second, in things that have different forms; in the third, in things that are ordered toward one and the same form.

Of the first kind, we say that—since the perfection of a thing arises through the form and not through the matter—whatever reaches the same form has also reached the same perfection, because it finds itself at the goal of its movement <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "movement" (motus) refers to any change from potentiality to actuality.</note>. And it is not of such perfection or imperfection that we speak regarding metals.

Of the second kind, we say that in such things which have manifold forms that are distinct in themselves and not ordered toward one another, those that have nobler forms than others also have more perfect forms than them; just as a human is called more perfect than a horse, and a horse more perfect than a donkey. And of this perfection and imperfection, we likewise do not speak regarding metals, although we could to some extent apply such a category to metals.

Of the third kind, we say that everything which is still in motion toward the form to which it is primarily ordained <note>Destined or naturally directed toward.</note> must be called imperfect; but when it is at the end of its movement, it must be called perfect. ### Refutation of the Objections.

Because, therefore, gold alone has already reached the end of the movement <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "movement" refers to the process of change toward a final goal or "actuality."</note> and has been formed according to the noblest and true *intention* <note>original: *Intention*</note> of nature, it alone can be called perfect. Nevertheless, they are not at the final goal of movement, in which the primary perfection consists.

Through this it becomes clear to what extent there are different *degrees* <note>original: *Gradus*</note> in the forms according to the opinion of the ancients, and to what extent there are not. It also becomes clear at the same time that in metals, one actually encounters no more than one form—namely, that of gold—because they do not become perfect under that transitory form. Therefore, at the final goal of movement, nature strips them of that form and brings them back into their primary *matter* <note>original: *Materia*; the formless base substance of all things.</note>, and transforms them into perfect gold, and there it comes to a stop. However, we do not say that the generation of imperfect metals results from an accident that occurs in nature, or from a specific intent caused by hindering factors—as some ancients and moderns have imagined, and as we also allowed ourselves to be persuaded (for the reasons already mentioned). Thus, some have already held the opinion that nature generates no gold except insofar as a transformation occurs through the *dispositions* <note>original: *Dispositiones*; the internal qualities or arrangements of matter.</note>, *natures*, and *forms* of the imperfect metals. ### Refutation of the Objections.

From the experience gained in minerals, however, it clearly appears that the transformation of imperfect metals is daily brought closer to gold by nature; therefore, one also very often finds mixed mineral veins. For the miners find in several tin and lead veins the essence of silver, which is found to be pure during refining and assaying; and in several ore and iron veins, they find the pure essence of gold—although this perhaps occurs quite rarely in iron veins due to their great impurity and distance from gold. Furthermore, in several silver veins, one finds the purest essence of gold, such as in the Kingdom of *Serbia*, that is, *Rascia*, which lies in *Slavonia* <note>Historically, these regions in the Balkans were famous for "electrum" or silver-gold ores.</note>. These are also at the same time so united by nature with one another that one cannot see the gold—indeed, it all looks like silver—yet through the assay, which is performed with sulfur in the fire, one separates the gold from the silver. From this, it is evident that all metals are on the path toward being transformed into gold. Consequently, in Germany and other places, imperfect silver has often been found in abundance within the mineral veins, which due to a lack of heat has suffered *scatelin* <note>Likely an archaic technical term referring to stunted growth or a "chilling" of the metal that stops its maturation.</note>, that is, which has not been *digested* <note>In alchemy, "digestion" is the process of maturing a substance through gentle, consistent heat, similar to how food is broken down or how a chick develops in an egg.</note>. In such cases, those who understand minerals say and advise that it should be left alone until the thirtieth degree and even further; and thus the experienced recognize that it must undergo *optesis* <note>original: *optesis*; a Greek term for "cooking" or "roasting," referring here to the final stage of mineral maturation.</note>, that is, a perfect *digestion* by the heat of the mineral veins, and then it will become true silver.

Therefore, *Geber* <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the most famous figure in Arabic alchemy, whose works were foundational to European science.</note> said in the *Chapter on the Nature of the Sun* <note>original: *Capitel de natura solis*; in alchemy, the "Sun" always refers to Gold.</note> that ore-scales flow from the ore veins into the rivers along with the sand; and when the flow of water stops, such ore-scales are cooked and *digested* in the sand through the thirtieth degree by the heat of the sun and the dryness of the sand, among which the very purest gold has been found. # Refutation of the Objections.

...it looks like a vein in the stone; but sometimes also like a vein passing through the earth, and this is purer than the aforementioned; sometimes finally it appears as sticky, moist lumps, and this is the purest of all. But lead and tin are sometimes found in stones, and sometimes in incorporated earth; sometimes mercury is also found running with them, as some say. Ore is also found incorporated into the stones as if they were **ore-druses** <term>Erß-Drusen: clusters of crystals that form inside a rock cavity or "vug"</term>; likewise iron is found this way. All of these must be ground with the strongest mills and **calcined** <note>original: *calciniret*. The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to remove impurities or change its chemical state.</note>, then refined and purified by fire. Miners have often found gold at last in the very same mountain-vein from which they initially dug silver. And that is the start of the origin of the gold-vein, and there the silver-vein ends, just as if in its **beginning** <note>original: *Principio*. Referring to the fundamental source or first principle of the mineral's existence.</note>.

Sometimes, however, this gold is in a stone, and the stone has an open hole that seems to catch a higher stone in which silver followed in a certain sequence. Therefore, this very same matter has, as it were, evaporated out of that same place; however, nature preserves the purer part at its origin, while the impurer part rises up through evaporation and **sublimation** <note>original: *Sublimation*. In alchemy, the process where a solid turns into a vapor and then solidifies again, used here to explain how "rising" minerals deposit in upper layers of rock.</note> toward that same stone. Thus, the different **digestion** <note>original: *Digestion*. An alchemical term for the "cooking" or ripening of a substance over time through gentle heat, much like biological digestion.</note> and purification has produced a different kind of metal.

From all that has been said so far, it becomes clear what sort and how great the difference between metals truly is—not only in their form, but also in their matter and **accidental properties** <note>original: *Accidentibus*. In classical philosophy, these are qualities like color or weight that can change without changing the essential nature of the thing itself.</note>, and both **actually** <note>original: *actu*.</note> and **potentially** <note>original: *potentiâ*.</note>. Because they differ only a very little from one another—both in their closely related and distant matter, and in the mixture itself as well as the manner of that mixing—their difference, even if it is found in the form itself, cannot properly be a difference of "species," such as exists between a human being and a horse. Rather, their differences are more properly understood as stemming from the matter and its parts: namely, to what extent it allows itself to be changed or not, and whether it is perfect or imperfect. For they are all made of exactly the same closely related matter, but the unchanged and imperfect ones are simply those destined to become gold.

# Refutation of the Objections.

And just as it is not necessary that which is unchanged—but which finds itself upon the path of **digestion** <term>Digestion: in alchemy, a process of slow, gentle heating that mimics the maturation of substances in the stomach or the earth</term>—should immediately return to the **beginning** <note>original: *Principio*</note> of digestion; so it is also not necessary that it be brought back again to its first—that is, its most closely related—**matter** <note>original: *Materie*</note>. Therefore, since the imperfect metals find themselves upon the continuous path of digestion and have not yet been fully changed, it will not be necessary for them to be brought back to the first principle of digestion or into their "first matter." Rather, one must only proceed with the digestion until they become gold. 

But in those things which do not possess this **step-by-step** <note>original: *per gradus*</note> order and natural capacity, it is necessary that they be brought back to their first matter. For example, if a human is to arise from an ox or from **wheat** <note>original: *Weißen* (archaic spelling of *Weizen*). The author argues that biological life must be broken down into "seed" before it can become something else.</note>, it is necessary that they be consumed, digested, and become the first matter of man, which is the **seed** <note>original: *Saame*</note> from which a human grows. Therefore, **Art** <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy—the human practice of accelerating natural processes.</note> has not labored to transform living and growing things, nor their parts, nor the minerals distant from this, into gold—just as Nature has never undertaken such a thing—because such a task is impossible for both the matter and the Art, unless they are first brought into the first—that is, the closely related or proximate—matter. Thus, Art follows Nature in this, in that it seeks to act like Nature, and it elevates Nature quite wonderfully; for Art is not opposed to Nature, but rather offers it a helping hand.

Now that the **distinctions** <note>original: *Distinctiones*</note> and generations of the metals have been shown and considered, the resolution of the **Philosopher’s** <note>original: *Philosophi*. Likely referring to Aristotle, whose theories of matter dominated alchemical thought.</note> fifth objection is clear. For Nature—after she has stripped the matter of the imperfect metals of that changeable form which they possessed in the **mountain-veins** <note>original: *Berg-Adern*</note>—transforms that same matter in a single moment into the form for which it was intended, namely gold. And thus she brings the metals back into the first matter—that is, matter stripped of all other forms—and so transforms them into gold.

# Refutation of the Objections.

->Aa 3<-

**Art** <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy—the human practice of accelerating or perfecting natural processes.</note> proceeds in the same way; for although the metals are not brought back to their first matter through melting alone, the matter is nevertheless purified and stripped of its previous form and all other forms through the addition, **influence**, and mixing of the **Philosopher's Stone**, which is the very **form** <note>In this context, "form" is the philosophical essence that makes a substance what it is (e.g., the "form" of gold makes matter gold).</note> of gold. The transformation into the form for which they were intended happens in that very same moment—namely, into the form of gold—because without the melting of metals, neither the influence, nor the mixing, nor the transformation by the transforming **medicine** <note>original: *Medicin*; another term for the Philosopher's Stone or Elixir.</note> can occur. In this way, they are brought back to their first matter and are transformed from one species into another according to the course of nature through **generation and decay** <note>original: *Zeugung und Verwesung*; the natural cycle of birth and breakdown.</note>. 

For when the [original] form is suppressed and mixed with the matter, the matter necessarily becomes bare; then, the generation and transformation into the specific final form occurs. This is because no new form can be generated in a prepared thing except through the destruction of that which was previously within it. Therefore, two **substantial forms** <note>original: *wesentliche Formen*; the essential identity of a substance.</note> will not exist in one matter at the same time, but only the one which has been newly brought into it—which is not accidental, but substantial. 

Similarly, if we wish to make **glass** from **Jupiter** <note>original: *Jove*; the alchemical name for Tin.</note> or **Saturn** <note>original: *Saturno*; the alchemical name for Lead.</note>, we must bring them back to their first matter, though they are not thereby brought to perfection. Thus, there is one kind of "return to the first matter" when one makes them perfect, because they then retain their primary general name [as metals] and only receive a new name for their actual species to which they were destined—namely, gold. There is another kind of return when one makes something else out of them, such as glass, etc.; then, they lose both their general name [metal] and the name of their own species to which they were ordained and in which they previously existed. Therefore, through Art, they are brought back to their first matter according to the orderly course of Nature—where everything happens step by step—just as Nature does, and not as they [the critics] imagine.

<meta>This page continues the logical defense of alchemical transformation by addressing specific counter-arguments regarding the nature of matter. # Refutation of the Objections.

To other objections, however, which assume the four elements to be the first—that is, the proximate matter—we answer thus and say: that the transformation of one thing into another can be understood in two ways. In the first way, insofar as the thing that is to be transformed is found in the first principle of the goal from which the movement begins; and this is the **first matter**, which is the **Chaos**, the beginning and origin of all elements. 

In the other way, insofar as it has already moved forward through many—indeed, most—changes from the starting point of the movement, and has been placed into a very near capacity to attain that <term>species<note>original: *Speciem*; here meaning the specific type or essential form of a substance.</note></term> into which it is to be transformed; so that after a small change has occurred, the form is generated. 

And that is chiefly called a **proximate matter**, which follows the first matter in order; just as we say that the elements are the first matter of man. However, the food made from the elements is even closer, or the proximate matter; but the blood arising from the food is even closer; the seed coming from the blood is closer still; and finally, the piece of flesh generated from such seed is the very nearest matter. 

Therefore, if the objection assumes the four elements to be the first matter, it concludes nothing against us; because, if a human is to be made from the elements, it must necessarily happen through those <term>dispositions<note>original: *Dispositiones*; the specific physical states or arrangements required for matter to transition from one form to another.</note></term> that we have mentioned. 

However, if a human is to be made from the seed, it is not necessary that it be brought back and dissolved into the first matter—which are the four elements—nor into the blood, nor into the food (because in such a way one would deviate from a form already brought toward perfection); rather, the <term>digestion<note>original: *Digestion*; in alchemy and early biology, this refers to the "ripening" or maturation of a substance through heat, similar to how a chick develops in an egg.</note></term> must only be continued until the matter takes on the form of a human. 

Likewise, if gold is to be made from the elements, they must necessarily pass through the ordained <term>dispositions</term> and means; namely, that in the beginning, out of them, a tough and heavy water, mixed with a very subtle sulfurous earth, [is formed...]

However the first matter may be assumed, all metals must nonetheless be **resolved** into that same first—that is, bare—matter, if they are to be transformed into Gold.

For the melting of metals alone does not **resolve** <note>original: *reſolviret*; to break down or reduce a substance to its most basic components.</note> them into their first—that is, pure—**matter**, as the objection rightly concludes; rather, it clearly shows the **matter** from which they are made, because every metal, when it has been melted, shows the nature and **accidents** <note>original: *Accidentia*; in Aristotelian philosophy, these are the non-essential properties like color or liquidity, as opposed to the essential substance.</note> of mercury. But as far as **Art** <note>The "Art" of Alchemy, or the manual intervention of the alchemist.</note> is concerned, they are of the same **disposition**, and the same amount of time belongs to them. For since only the mercury of the **imperfect metals** is transformed into gold by the **Elixir**, after it has first been purified of the corrupting sulfur—and yet the mercury of the **common masses** <note>original: *gemeinen Pöbels*; referring to ordinary quicksilver found in shops, which alchemists believed was already relatively pure compared to the mercury trapped inside solid lead or copper.</note> requires no such purification; **therefore** <note>original: *Ergo*</note> it must, through such purification, return to the same **matter**. For its **coagulation** <note>The state of being solid or frozen.</note> does not prevent the equality of its nature with the nature of that same substance; therefore, there will be the same **disposition** and the same time for their perfection, because the increased power and strength of the **Elixir**, which expands continuously, **extends** and pours itself over both in an instant, and makes them no less perfect, in that it imparts **digestion** to both through its own overflowing and increased **digestion**, which it possesses in such a way that **digestion** can occur in both. And thus we have reached the end of this question, along with the proper explanation. Thanks be given to **GOD** for this.

### To Which This Art Belongs.

Since the art of making gold is a real <term>entity<note>original: "Ens." A philosophical term for something that exists in reality.</note></term>, it must necessarily belong to one branch of philosophy. However, it does not belong under Mathematics, because the art of making gold deals with a real being that is bound to movement and matter. Nor does it belong under Metaphysics, or divine discipline, because that does not deal with a real being that is separated from movement and matter, such as the **Intelligences** <note>original: "Intelligentiæ." In medieval philosophy, these were spiritual beings or "movers" (like angels) that existed without physical bodies.</note> etc. Thus, it must necessarily be drawn toward natural philosophy or **Physics**, because that field deals with a real being that is bound to movement and matter. Likewise, natural things also require a certain matter for themselves, just as smell requires the nose, or sight requires the eye; and therefore they cannot be recognized without their matter or <term>subject<note>original: "Subjecto." The underlying material substance in which a property resides.</note></term>. But those things that belong to Mathematics require no specific matter for themselves—such as a line, a triangle, or a number—because such <term>entities<note>original: "Entia."</note></term> can exist in any matter, and this is because they can be recognized in any circumscribed matter. But the entities in Metaphysics or divine science, because they have no matter, do not require any matter for their contemplation, and are thus recognized in a spiritual manner.

Furthermore, it is to be known that all arts take their beginning and origin from the sciences, and stem from them either directly or indirectly. For the <term>principle<note>original: "Principium." The fundamental source or starting point.</note></term> of the sciences is the Understanding, insofar as it either contemplates something or works something. The principle of the arts, which deal with such an entity as one imagines in the Reason, is the Understanding, insofar as it contemplates something. And just as the principle of Nature is the Understanding, for which reason Nature, as well as its principles and works, are always truthful, because they stem from the Understanding, and the Understanding from the Divine Being, in which all truth shines forth and from which all truth flows, because that same being is Truth itself. # On the Principles of Metals.

In moisture—that is, the element of water—one essentially and primarily finds the property of being contained by a foreign boundary <note>This refers to Aristotle’s definition of liquids in *On Generation and Corruption*: they have no shape of their own and must be held by a container.</note>. This same containment is found in all metals when they are melted; therefore, etc. Likewise, those things which coagulate and freeze from the cold have in their first matter an exceeding abundance of watery moisture, as is stated in the *fourth book of Meteorology* <note>original: "quarto meteororum"; Aristotle’s *Meteorology* was the standard text for explaining the formation of minerals in the earth.</note>; such are the metals and other similar things. And because watery moisture easily evaporates from the fire, but metals retain their moisture even in great fires, the moisture of metals is therefore not simply water, but rather water insofar as it is mixed with other elements. However, for the nature of water to remain truly within the metals, it must be viscous and oily so that it can persist, as can be seen in the nourishing moisture or <term>Chyle</term> <note>original: "Chylo"; in medicine, chyle is the milky fluid containing fats produced during digestion. Here, it refers to the "nutritive" essence that sustains the "body" of the metal.</note> of living things. And because we see that viscous and oily moisture in most things is easily ignited and is not separated from the fire until it is entirely consumed, yet such moisture is not found in metals, it does not seem that a purely viscous and oily moisture is the matter of metals, except insofar as it is mixed with earthy parts.

Therefore, it is to be noted that in the generation of metals there is a double moisture: one is viscous and external, which does not reach a total union with the earthy parts of a thing, and this is sulfurous and can easily be ignited; the other, however, is an internal viscous moisture, and this is unique, and is thoroughly of one kind with the earthy parts; and this can be neither ignited nor burned, because it is exactly matched within its most delicate earthy parts and mixed through a strong union. Indeed, it is mixed in such a way that the smallest part of the one has become identical with the smallest part of the other, and the greatest part of the one has become identical with the greatest part of the other; and they are thus [transformed] by their own <term>Digestion</term> <note>original: "Digestion"; in alchemy, this is the process of exposing a substance to gentle, consistent heat to ripen or mature it, mimicking the heat of the stomach or the earth.</note>

# On the Principles of Metals.

...[Natur-]es <note>The text begins mid-word, likely completing "Natures" from the previous page.</note> she has provided such sulfur that cannot be melted, yet nevertheless coagulates, as in **marcasite**, **magnesia** <note>In this context, magnesia refers to various mineral ores, often manganese or a form of lead, rather than modern magnesium.</note>, and **antimony** <note>original: *Spießglas*, the historical term for stibnite or antimony ore.</note>. The sulfur in marcasite is not "fixed," and can therefore be burned; however, in antimony, it is fixed <note>original: *figiret*; in alchemy, a "fixed" substance is one that can withstand fire without evaporating or changing.</note> and cannot be burned.

Thus, the first, near, closest, and actual matter of all metals is **mercury**—not in its natural state, but insofar as it is coagulated in the mineral hollows of the earth by the specific active agent, namely **sulfur** (which can be melted), and is mixed with the sulfur itself. Therefore <note>original: *Ergo*</note>, this matter—or one entirely similar to it—must be the matter of silver, if generation is to occur from a capable and closely related substance. 

One must therefore necessarily say that these two things, when mixed together, are the principles <note>original: *Principia*, the fundamental building blocks</note> of both Art <note>Referring to the "Art" of Alchemy.</note> and Nature. Because they agree in their closely related matter, in the active agent, and in the manner of their mixing, they possess a **circular generation** <note>original: *Circular-Zeugung*; the idea that substances can be transformed into one another in a continuous cycle.</note> relative to one another, as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemical wisdom.</note>, **Rasis** <note>Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi, a major Persian alchemist and physician.</note>, and other philosophers have stated. For just as the elements differ very little from their first matter from which they arise, and are thus generated circularly against one another, so it is also with the metals, though in a slightly different way. 

Because the generation of metals is reciprocal <note>original: *reciproca*</note>—meaning that one can afterwards be transformed into another because of their similar perfection and small distance from their first matter—one is no more ordered toward the other than the reverse. In the metals, however, it is different, because they are all inherently imperfect, except for **gold** alone—that is, in a certain degree of imperfection. And they are all ordered toward gold alone, as if toward the ultimate final goal <note>original: *lezten Endzweck*</note>; therefore, they do not return to their previous form once they have become gold. The sign of their transformation into gold by Nature is their mixing within a mountain vein <note>original: *Berg-Ader*, a mineral-rich fissure in the earth where ores are found.</note>,

Since, therefore, the Philosopher's Stone <note>The legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold.</note> actually transforms the matter after the preceding changes, it alone can make gold, and this is consistent with reason. ## In which entire Treatise the Secret of Nature is incorporated.

We wish to say once more: that if in one thing only two composite parts are found, and one of these composite parts is found without the other, it is also necessary that the remaining part be found without the first. Just as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and early modern texts.</note> proves in the eighth book of the *Physics* <note>original: "octavo physicorum"</note>: Regarding that which is moved and that which moves—in such a case, because the "moved" is found without the "mover," it follows that the "mover" must also necessarily be found without the "moved." From this it becomes clear that if one of the composite parts were separated from such a composite thing, the other part must also necessarily—if it is to be separated—be separated elsewhere in another place.

-># Main Principles of this Art.<-

...purified; from which—on account of different **digestion** <term>Digestion: In alchemy, a process of slow, consistent heating used to mature or "ripen" a substance.</term>, skill, and proportion of the mixed things (consisting in quantity, quality, place, and time)—each distinct metal is generated according to its specific purpose. And just as the form produced by Art is distinct from the composite essence produced by Nature—even though both are ordained toward one main goal—it appears fitting that the governance of Art should differ from the governance of Nature. This difference lies not in the **matter**, but in the **digestion**, heat, place, time, skill, and proportion of the mixed things. Accordingly, it seems that the **digestion**, the location, and the origin of the generation of metals—that is, the forms of the metals, specifically gold—along with other circumstances, is indeed possible through Art. Therefore, if the **digestion** (as previously stated) and the location or the artificial instrument are equal to the natural ones, then it is necessarily possible for the Art to make gold, in regards to both location and digestion. 

And because digestion is brought to perfection by internal natural heat, and external warmth is equal to the natural in that it assists it; **therefore** <note>original: "Ergo"</note> the external warmth in **Alchemy** will come to the aid of the natural heat so that it may perfectly digest those metals which are not yet digested; **therefore** <note>original: "Ergo"</note> the Art is possible. ### The Fourth Ground of Proof.

Fourthly, it is concluded thus: Whatever is found in the middle of a movement while assuming a form can also be brought to the goal of such movement, where it is not prevented. ## Objection: Whether sulfur is a material part of gold and of the Philosopher’s Stone.

However, one might say: It seems to follow from your words that sulfur, together with mercury, could be a material part of gold and the Philosopher’s Stone—which you have nevertheless denied. ### Chapter on the nature of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi"</note>:

And for that reason, such sulfur—because it is added during generation and through some community with external sulfur—is mixed with the quicksilver <note>original: "Queckſilber"</note> and coagulates <term>coagulate: to thicken or solidify a liquid into a solid mass</term> it; and neither of the two sulfurs is fixed <term>fixed: a state where a substance is stable and no longer evaporates or changes when heated</term>, yet each of them coagulates and colors the quicksilver. Therefore, it does not enter into the gold, and consequently can be neither the matter nor even a part of the matter of the Stone <term>Stone: the Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold</term>, nor can it tinge <term>tinge: to infuse with color or transformative power; to apply a tincture</term> it, just as this does not occur in mineral gold.

By this, a very great secret in this Art is revealed: namely, that quicksilver is not coagulated or colored by such a coagulation as occurs through mixing, except only with sulfur—but solely with its own internal sulfur which serves its perfection. With external sulfur, however, it is coagulated and colored toward corruption <note>original: "Verweſung"; in alchemy, this refers to the breakdown or impurity of a metal rather than its perfection</note>. Whatever, therefore, coagulates the quicksilver—in whatever way it may happen—coagulates it through the power of sulfur, such as the vapor of Saturn <note>Saturn is the alchemical name for lead; "vapor of Saturn" refers to lead fumes which were known to solidify mercury</note>, the juices of the earth, and other such things; because it could not happen that two things distinct in their essence could have the same effect in the same way upon something else, unless it happened through one thing that is common to both. I mean, however, the coagulation which occurs through mixing alongside the preservation of the metallic melt. Therefore, if any other things—whether they be mineral, vegetable, or animal—coagulate it, they are foreign to it and coagulate and color it differently, because it does not happen according to the true nature, but only in a common way. Thus, through a deeply hidden and divine Art, we must produce the true silver <note>In alchemy, "silver" (Luna) often represents the white stage of the Work that precedes the "gold" (Solar) stage.</note> from quicksilver alone by means of the operation of the external sulfur naturally mixed with it, and coagulate <term>coagulate: to solidify or thicken a liquid substance</term> it without that same sulfur, because the generating thing cannot be a material part of the generated thing. For such a thing will be of an easy metallic melting, which is both very delicate, after the manner of a cause, and also remains stable above the strife and the violence of the fire, and will very quickly transform all metals into perfect gold by following nature. For because it contains within itself all degrees of perfection without deficiency or excess, it will transform all metals into a medium, which is gold.

### Objection regarding sulfur.

For God has preferred sulfur above all stones / therefore He has preferred the same among us / and among the ignorant it is of little value *etc.* Likewise, Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jābir ibn Hayyān, an 8th-century polymath often considered the father of chemistry.</note> in the chapter *on the nature of sulfur* <note>original: "de natura sulphuris"</note>: The same illuminates every body through the gift of the Most High God / because it is an alum and a tincture <term>tincture: a substance capable of permeating and changing the color or quality of another</term> *etc.* Likewise Bulus in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among Greek philosophers.</note>: The pure water is from sulfur alone / yet not from sulfur solely and alone / but from several things / which have become a sulfur *etc.* Likewise Anaxagoras in the aforementioned place: You should know / that the perfection of this work is the water of sulfur. Likewise Pythagoras in the mentioned place: You should know / that our *composition* <note>original: "Composition"</note> is nothing other / than the water of sulfur / and the pure water of sulfur comes from sulfur alone. The very same in the stated place: The entire perfection of the work occurs / when one sulfur is contained within the other. And briefly, it appears / that all *philosophers* <note>original: "Philosophi"</note> desire this.

To this question we answer / as above / namely / that in quicksilver <term>quicksilver: another name for mercury, considered the "mother" of all metals</term> alone lies the entire perfection. And because the same, in its *composition*, has sulfurous dry parts / which tincture and color it / and indeed with the white color in deed <note>Referring to the "Albedo" or white stage of the alchemical process.</note> / but with the red *potentially* <note>original: "potentiâ"</note>. Therefore this sulfur makes the same perfect / and gives it the form. And because it cannot bring itself forth in deed / nature has therefore mixed with it the external sulfur in its mines / so that she may decoct <term>decoct: to mature or "cook" a substance using heat to achieve perfection</term> it / and bring it from *potentiality* into the actual *act* <note>original: "Actum"</note>. In the same way, Art also works just as Nature. And because the watery moisture and the earthy sulfurous dryness have become entirely one and the same in it in every way / therefore it either remains with its whole being in the fire / or yields with its whole being from the fire / because the part of the one will not leave the other / as Geber says. possesses a little of the mercury from which it has obtained its luster, as well as the property that it can be **extended** <note>original: "extenderet"; referring to malleability, or the ability to be hammered thin.</note> under the hammer; but from the sulfur alone it receives its essence, its color, and also the capacity to be cast, along with the other specific **accidental properties** <note>original: "Accidentia"; in the philosophy of the time, these were non-essential characteristics like color, smell, or hardness that distinguish one substance from another.</note>. Likewise, mercury finds no **entry** <note>original: "Ingreß"</note> therein, except insofar as it makes the matter fit for **extension** [malleability], namely, in the same way that cold has its **entry** in a work of nature; for the true **instrument** <note>original: "Instrument"</note> of nature is heat, and not cold. Therefore, those who have directed their **operations** <note>original: "Operationes"</note> toward the sulfur of the common man <note>referring to ordinary yellow chemical sulfur as opposed to the "philosophical sulfur" sought by alchemists.</note> have always been fruitless in their endeavor. 

In explaining this, however, we say—not only according to the truth of this science, but also according to astrological and other sciences, and no less according to the opinion of all the ancient **philosophers** <note>original: "Philosophorum"</note>—that all the ancient philosophers established the number of metals according to the number of the wandering stars or **planets** <note>original: "Planeten"</note>, because the metals also possess a wandering motion. And because these planets are 7 in number, they also found 7 metals, which they attributed to those same planets as the original causes that set the metals in motion; for they correspond with one another as higher causes do with their lower effects. 

Therefore, lead is assigned to **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturno"</note>, tin to **Jupiter** <note>original: "Jovi"</note>, iron to **Mars** <note>original: "Marti"</note>, gold to the Sun, copper/bronze <note>original: "Erz"; specifically referring here to copper, the metal of Venus.</note> to **Venus** <note>original: "Veneri"</note>, and silver to the Moon. To **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio"</note>, however, they assigned no metal, because no more than the aforementioned 6 are found—namely, those which have reached **coagulation** <note>original: "Coagulation"; the process of solidifying into a stable form.</note> by means of melting and **extension** [malleability]. And for that reason, the philosophers then hit upon the actual matter from which the metals take their origin—since the matter itself is their essence—and all said that this was mercury, which they assigned to **Mercury**. Thus, compelled by the truth itself, they included the raw matter of the metals within the number of the metals, so that they might [fulfill] <note>The word "erfülle" (fulfill) is completed from the catchword on the following page.</note> their number according to the number of the planets.

And because such matter is indeed most necessary, it must also necessarily be very well recognized if the matter is to attain the form of gold. Therefore, it appears that in every mixed thing, earth and water are abundant <note>original: *überflüssig*; here meaning they form the visible, physical bulk that contains the inner spirits.</note>.
