Opposing qualities are treated in the same way, so that the moist and the dry are equal in their powers, as are the hot and the cold. They become altogether one without any distinction, and thus the mixed being is **stabilized** <note>original: *continuiret*; meaning the substance remains in its state without further unwanted change.</note>, for there is no conflict or **opposition** <note>original: *Contrarietät*</note> there, but rather a total **oneness** <note>original: *Identität*</note> and equality of the **composing** elements.

Regarding the elements, we say, according to the opinion of the alchemists, that the elements in this art are the moist and the dry—that is, water and earth—and that air is found within the water, while fire is found within the earth. For this reason, an artist must thoroughly recognize the simple elements before he undertakes their composition, so that he knows how to correctly assemble them for the production of the composite thing. Therefore, just as the dough <note>original: "Pasta"</note> cannot become a ferment <term>Ferment: a substance, like yeast in bread, that transforms the nature of the material it is added to; in alchemy, it is the "seed" of gold</term> without its internal leaven: so too the stone can neither be fermented nor brought to perfection and fulfillment without this hidden spiritual body.

Although in truth the stone itself—according to its entire essence, its body, its soul, and its spirit—is always one and the same regarding the matter itself: yet the Philosophers call it now this and now that, according to different relations and thoughts. And this is what Plato intended when he said that matter flows unceasingly unless the Form <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "Form" gives shape and purpose to "Matter"</note> stops the flow; for the body must restrain the soul so that it does not flow away. 

And thus Rosinus <term>Rosinus: the Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Egyptian-Greek alchemist</term> and the ancients first understood it when they said: Every body that finds a soul takes it in quite easily. And from this, Plato prophesied as if of the Day of Judgment, saying in the fourth book of *The Stoics* <note>original: "in quarto stollicarum"</note>, and Hamec in his commentary there: The soul must be united with its first body from which it came, and not with another; if you do not do this, your endeavor will fail you, as it does most of the ignorant, and this is because they do not know this secret.

When it [the substance] can fly away from the fire, it is called the Soul; but when it can remain in the fire and persist constantly, it is called the Body. 

If, therefore, at the time of generation the soul stands in the fire and its powers remain through the power of the Spirit, then it flies from the fire and also takes the body with it in such volatility. Thus, he who operates remains without the actual effect of his intention; he waits for that which has already come and also gone away again, and which otherwise will never return—and such seems wondrous to him <note>The author is describing a common alchemical failure: when the material "vanishes" or evaporates out of the flask because the heat was not properly managed.</note>.

But if the powers of the body then have preference over the powers of the soul, because of the tempered equality of the Spirit (which has been brought from actual deed to a total capacity), then the body retains the soul with itself, so that it never has the power to fly away from the fire. Then he who operates has achieved his intention, as the **Ancients** held. Then the Spirit remains always with them, sometimes in the actual deed, sometimes in the total capacity. All of this can be gathered from the words of **Plato** <note>The Greek philosopher was often cited as a legendary alchemical authority in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> in the **Assembly of the Philosophers** <note>original: "turba Philosophorum," one of the most famous early Latin alchemical texts, written around 900 AD, depicting a debate among ancient sages.</note> and in the **Stollicis** <note>original: "stollicis"; likely a reference to a specific section or perhaps a distorted title of an alchemical work.</note>.

But I cannot reasonably imagine this to be so, except in this way alone...

**Places:** Every seed that is cast into the earth grows forth according to its kind; if different kinds of seed are mixed together, each grows forth according to its own kind, etc. For things produce nothing but things like themselves, and bring forth no other but their own fruits, etc. Likewise <term>Senior</term> <note>Zadith ben Hamuel (c. 900–960), a significant Arabic alchemist whose works were translated into Latin and became foundational for European alchemy</note>: Minerals are not nourished so that they should depart from their origin; rather, they return to that from which they have come, and are not transformed from this into something else, and whoever says otherwise speaks untruth. In the same way, it must also be understood here, namely by way of parable, because the entire discourse of this art has been conducted through parables and allegories, etc.

# Of the Ferment of the Stone.

Furthermore, for a better understanding of the aforementioned things, it should be noted that the operations of heat in generation <gloss>the creation of something new</gloss> and decay <gloss>the breaking down of matter</gloss>, insofar as it is merely heat, are not determined or ordained toward a specific and obvious end goal, except insofar as the heat is governed by the soul or the intellect. This is because heat is the instrument of the soul, and every acting thing arranges and measures its instrument so that it may introduce the form <note>In Aristotelian terms, "form" is the essential identity or design of an object that makes it what it is</note>. 

By heat, however, I mean that which is actually present—as in animals, which possess it in reality—or that which can be present, as in plants, minerals, and certain living things which possess it figuratively speaking. This heat is elementary, heavenly, and likewise mixed among itself in compound things. Therefore the <term>Philosopher</term> <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle</note> says in the second book of *Physics* <note>original Latin: "secundo physicorum"</note>: "A man and the sun beget a man." This is because without this double heat <note>The internal heat of the biological parent and the external heat of the sun</note>, generation does not occur. 

Such heat is measured according to its quantity, quality, and duration by the soul or the intellect—or by both—in all natural things, toward a certain end goal in which the attainment of the form consists. Therefore, because <term>Alchemy</term> is an imitator of nature and operates in fact by means of heat—namely fire—the soul of the artist <note>The "artist" here refers to the alchemist performing the work</note> must necessarily modify and measure that same heat according to quantity, quality, and time, until a certain determined goal for the attainment of the form is reached. There is always a certain determined time between the active agent and the passive subject <note>The "active agent" is the alchemist or the fire; the "passive subject" is the raw material being transformed</note> in which the form is introduced. Now, if the soul of the artist does not measure the heat of the fire in this way, but continues it beyond the goal, then the fire will necessarily destroy the form which it had created. This happens because not everything was well-measured. This point has been clearly enough proven above: the power of fire is infinite, but the soul of the artist must measure it and enclose it within certain bounds, etc.

# What the Theriack Is, and What the *Poison* <note>original Latin: "Venenum"</note> in the Stone of the Wise Is Called.

## The Fifth Chapter.

Because the ancient *Philosophers* <note>The alchemists of old</note> included both the theriack <note>Historically a "universal antidote" or medicine; here used metaphorically for an alchemical agent</note> and the *poison* <note>original Latin: "Venenum"</note> in the *composition* of the Stone of the Wise: and because these *terms* <note>original Latin: "Termini"</note> are among the most hidden *terms* of this Art, we wish to speak of them now. We say, therefore, that just as the *ferment* <note>original Latin: "Fermentum"</note> was understood in two ways, so also is the *poison*, because it has the same nature; likewise the theriack. Firstly, it refers to the perfect and completed Stone itself in its effect against the imperfect metals; in the other way, it refers to that which makes the Stone itself perfect. and this **coagulated** <term>coagulated: thickened or solidified from a liquid state</term> water they call by the name of each "little man"; afterward they wedded him to a woman, and he is from her, and she is the root and **coagulation** of the same, just as *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary mythical founder of alchemy</note> says, etc. The same author says in the mentioned place: This water, however, once it has curdled, also causes other things to curdle; and the flowing water is the mother of the curdled, and has come forth from the same, etc. In such a way, they have designated the man and the woman within their Stone, naming the woman the milk itself, which is **coagulated**, while calling the man that which does the **coagulating**, because acting is attributed to the man, but "suffering" <note>In the philosophical sense, "suffering" refers to being the passive recipient of an action</note> is attributed to the woman.

Therefore, *Alexander* <note>Likely referring to Alexander the Great, to whom many medieval alchemical works were apocryphally attributed</note> has said: You should know that no one is born except from man and woman, and no branch is brought forth except from the moist and warm, or else from the dry.

Thus, man and woman are joined together and become entirely one, etc. 

Likewise, another author in the mentioned place: Honor the king and his wife, and do not burn them, etc. *Senior* <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century alchemist known as "Senior" in Latin translations</note>: The man is found without wings beneath the woman, but the woman has wings and wishes to fly; the man, however, holds her back from flight. <note>In alchemical art, "wings" symbolize volatility—the tendency of a substance to evaporate. A figure without wings represents "fixation," or the ability to stay solid under heat.</note> And for this reason, the Philosophers have said: Make it so that the woman rises above the man, and then the man will also rise above the woman, etc. And *Rosinus*: The woman receives strength from the man, etc.

And it is to be known that the man and the woman are one and the same in a single **Subject** <term>Subject: translated from the Latin 'subjecto'; here referring to the underlying physical matter or substance</term>, and within such a unity of the Subject, they possess distinct and opposing powers. Therefore, when this same Stone arises, it contains in itself a mixture of man and woman; yet it arises fluid, truly flowing, volatile, soul, and undergoing the **coagulation** <term>coagulation: the process of a liquid thickening or becoming solid</term>, and thus it is the woman.

And just as the feminine, the "suffering" <note>the passive or receptive principle</note>, is something diminished and incomplete: so the masculine, because it is something active, is that which fulfills it and makes it perfect.

# The Birth of the Stone

...are not generated / except from things similar to them in nature / such as from their <term>principles</term> <note>the fundamental components of matter</note> and roots / according to the manner that we have described. Accordingly, the branch relates to the heart as something generated and separated from its seed / in which the entire power of the seed resides / which is capable of generating all the limbs of the plant and its parts according to the requirements of its species / just as the heart of a fruit is generated from the seed in the mother’s womb.

Therefore, just as the seed has nothing further to accomplish after the generation of the heart / because it has already introduced the form / and it is also impossible / for two active things to come together in the same way for one effect: So too must the external sulfur behave in the same way: *Therefore* <note>original: "Ergò"</note> the external sulfur must likewise / after it has effectively brought forth the sulfur from the hidden depths of the mercury / which is the heart and the form of the mercury / be separated from it.

We confirm this / through the statement of the **Philosopher** <note>A common title for Aristotle in medieval and early modern texts</note> in the 15th book of *On Animals* <note>original: "de animalibus"</note>, who says: "But the heart / or a member / which corresponds to the heart / is created first by the seed / which will be the beginning of the generation of the entire body, etc." And after this he says: "And for this reason, during the creation, the heart can actually be seen first among all the limbs / and is evident to the senses / as well as to the intellect: when it is conceived and awakened from the seed of the man and the <term>superfluity of the woman</term> <note>Refers to the Aristotelian theory that the male seed provides the form/spirit, while the female "superfluity" (menstrual blood) provides the material matter</note> / and is left alone / then it must govern itself like a son / who has gone out from his father's house, etc."

# Of Analogies

After what has been said, it is to be known / that / just as it is not necessary that the first moving cause <note>the initial force that starts a process, such as the creator or the starting chemical catalyst</note> touch its movable work without ceasing / but rather it is enough / that it has already touched it / just as can be seen with an archer and the arrow / so it also is with the seed / and that from which it was cut off / namely the heart / which the seed has generated / and the heart / which generates the limbs of the fruit of the womb. Therefore the Philosopher <note>a standard reference to Aristotle</note> says in the 16th book of *On Animals* <note>original: "de animalibus"</note>: Just as it happens to those things / which are in themselves / that they move the first moving thing / not / because they entirely touch the body of another thing / but because they have already touched it in past time: So it is also with that / from which the seed comes / and it touches it no further thereafter. <header>Letter of Bonus of Ferrara.</header>

# Now follows the letter of Bonus of Ferrara, an excellent and famous <term>Doctor of Medicine</term> <note>original: *Doctoris in der Medicin*; Petrus Bonus was a 14th-century physician and alchemist</note> and of this art, to one of his intimate friends.

Dearest Brother N. You have, in your writing and petitions, very urgently and with great devotion and trust, asked me to write to you concerning what the **matter** is for which the **philosophers** <note>In this context, "philosophers" refers specifically to alchemists or "natural philosophers"</note> in their investigation of **Alchemy** have taken such great pains, so that they might obtain the highly venerable **Stone** of the same with great diligence. Therefore, no one in this art will be able to speak the truth, nor instruct others with a firm foundation of truth, who does not first know the matter; for no one can judge a thing except he who has previously truly recognized it. 

Therefore, if I had not yet recognized the truth, I would not be able to fulfill your desire through my answer. Nevertheless, because in this art I have always preferred to hold to **reason** rather than to outward form—after I began to understand all this with the greatest difficulty and labor, and fell into many errors both in "sailing" <note>An alchemical metaphor for deep study or the "voyage" of the Great Work</note> and in passing by—I will now reveal to you which matter I am certain of, according to my opinion and conjecture, thereby fulfilling your desire and proving what I say with sufficiently probable reasons. For it is not enough to say that a thing is so, unless one also shows why it is so. 

And what I have said in general according to reason in that extensive inquiry which is called *The Precious New-Found Pearl* <note>original: *Margarita Pretiosa Novella*; the primary work of Petrus Bonus, written c. 1330</note> in the investigation of this art, and in the treatise against those who operate with an unsuitable matter—which I wrote under the name of **Brother Anselm the Monk**—I will now, moved by love for you, reveal to you specifically and in particular, so that you [may understand] the **intention of Hermes** <note>original: *Intention Hermetis*; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>,

# *Lacinus's Collections* <note>Janus Lacinius was a 16th-century editor who compiled the works of famous alchemists like Arnaldus.</note> from *Arnaldo de Villa Nova*, which encompass and correctly teach the composition of the Stone of the Wise.

Since we have already established the **theory** <note>original: "Theorie"</note> through what has already been said, our **intention** <note>original: "Intention"</note> now rests mainly in the **practice** <note>original: "Praxi"</note>. For in such sciences, as in others, the **experience** <note>original: "Experienz"</note> of practice can strengthen the truth of theory; nevertheless, it belongs to wisdom and science to consider things according to their causes, because experience is deceptive when knowledge has not preceded it. For among those who philosophize, there is a constant **meditation** <note>original: "Meditation"; here meaning deep intellectual contemplation or study.</note> that one should well consider what ought to happen before beginning a work. For it would be the greatest error if one wished to proceed to a work before having well considered the **practical application** <note>original: "Practicirung"</note> of it in one’s thoughts—an evaluation which theory itself produces in the soul. One must therefore study diligently before undertaking the labor of the hands, for the work follows nature, and not the other way around. **The First Chapter:** That there is only one Stone of the Wise / because there is only one essence and only one way of working / both in the **White** and the **Red** <note>The "White" work (albedo) results in silver, while the "Red" work (rubedo) results in gold.</note>, although in the red medicine an addition of yellow color is to be found / yet herefrom the medicine is not changed in its essence.

**The Third Chapter:** That it is very difficult / to find our **work** <note>The "Great Work" or *Magnum Opus* of alchemy.</note> only in the **first matter** <term>Prima Materia: the primitive, formless base of all matter that alchemists sought to isolate.</term> of the metals.

Therefore the philosophers say: Unless the **bodies** <note>The solid, physical metallic forms.</note> become no bodies / that is / not corporeal / but become **spiritual** <term>Spirit: a volatile substance or the refined essence of a metal.</term> / you will achieve nothing / for the dissolved bodies have been brought into the nature of spirits / even though they are more **fixed** <note>Fixed: stable in fire; resistant to evaporation.</note> than the spirits / although they are dissolved with them. For the dissolution of the body happens through the nature of the spirit / and the **congealing** <note>original: "Gerinnung"; the solidification of a liquid.</note> of the spirit happens with the dissolution of the body. And then the bodies are mixed with the spirits / or the body with the spirit / when they have been brought to a first nature.

# The Fifth Chapter: Concerning the investigation of the modes of action of the natural stone at the conclusion;

Note that there are four primary modes by which the natural stone is governed, namely: **dissolution**, **washing**, **restoring**, and **fixation**. **Dissolution** means the powerful refining of a substance and bringing it back into a simple essence; **washing** means bringing the dark essence back into a light one, and the moist into a dry one; **fixation** means causing the volatile <note>Volatile substances are those that easily evaporate or escape when heated; "fixing" them means making them stable and solid.</note> to hold fast to its body, and this occurs through dissolution and *coagulation* <note>original: "coaguliren"; the process of thickening or solidifying a liquid.</note>.

# The Sixth Chapter: Concerning the dissolution of the stone and its burial, which is its first governance; therein note this conclusion: that the stone must be dissolved by purified and restored *mercury* <note>original: "Mercurium"</note>, and after this be buried <note>In alchemy, "burial" or inhumation often refers to placing the vessel in a warm, dark place, such as horse manure or a sand bath, to maintain a gentle, steady heat for digestion.</note>; and this is done so that we may obtain the sulfur and mercury from that same matter from which gold and silver are made beneath the earth, so that from the same, etc.

# The Seventh Chapter: Concerning the second governance, which consists of washing and purification; namely, of the black, corrupted, and hideous, so that it may be very light and bright and clean from all filth.

Therefore, one must divide the stone according to its four elements <note>The four classical elements: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth, which alchemists believed composed all matter.</note>, and wash and purify each element. The Water is separated by distilling in *Mary’s Bath* <term>Balneo Mariæ: A water bath or double boiler used to provide gentle, even heat.</term>, but the Air is separated by distilling through the ashes, as is the Fire; the Earth remains sitting at the bottom, etc.

For thus says Arnold of Villanova <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311) was a famous physician and alchemist.</note>: It is true that all things that can be melted are naturally fashioned from mercury and the essence of sulfur, and this is because it is a property of mercury that it is *coagulated* <note>solidified</note> by the heat or the vapor of sulfur: because every dry thing naturally consumes its moisture: thus the mercury is coagulated by the vapor of sulfur, out of its earthly, subtle essence, which is airy and

# That There is Only One Philosopher’s Stone.

# That it is impossible for the Stone to become perfect from the essence or the matter of metals alone.

## The Third Chapter.

It is impossible for our Stone to reach perfection from the matter of metals alone; for if we were to begin our work in the first matter of Nature alone <note>The "first matter" (prima materia) is the raw, unformed base of all substances.</note>, it would take far too long and could not be brought to completion. Great and infinite costs would also be required to accomplish such a thing; and even if, finally, through heavy toil, the Stone were made from the nature of metals, the philosophical work would still not have even begun. This is because it is necessary that the Philosopher’s Stone be brought forth from the nature of two bodies before it becomes a perfect Elixir.

For it is necessary that that which is the Elixir be more purified and digested <term>digested</term><note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the process of exposing a substance to gentle, consistent heat over a long period, mimicking biological maturation.</note> than gold and silver. This is because the Elixir itself must transform all bodies devoid of perfection into gold or silver—a feat which gold and silver could not accomplish in the slightest on their own. For if they shared their perfection with another, they would become imperfect themselves, because they cannot tincture <term>tincture</term><note>To "tincture" is to permeate a base metal with the quality of a noble metal, changing its internal nature and color.</note> except only as far as their own substance extends.

Therefore, when the dry is transformed into the cold, the cold into the moist, the moist into the warm, and the warm into the dry, then you will have the entire art completely. 

There are, however, four primary modes of governance <note>original: "Regierung" — stages or chemical processes controlled by the alchemist.</note> which transform them into one another: Dissolving, Washing, Returning, and Fixation. 

*   **Dissolving** means bringing the strong into a simple essence and refining it <term>refining</term><note>original: "subtilisiren" — to make a substance pure, thin, or volatile.</note>.
*   **Washing** means [transforming] the dark into the light.
*   **Returning** means transforming the moist into the dry.
*   **Fixation** <term>Fixation</term><note>original: "Festmachen" — making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates when heated.</note>, however, is keeping the volatile with its body. 

In the same way, **Dissolving** happens through dividing, destroying, and returning to the first matter <term>first matter</term><note>original: "erste Materie" — the primordial, undifferentiated substance from which all metals were thought to grow.</note>; **Washing** [happens] through distilling, burying, and calcining <term>calcining</term><note>original: "calciniren" — heating a substance until it is reduced to a dry powder or "ash."</note>; **Returning** happens through mixing, fattening <note>original: "fett machen" — the alchemical process of "imbibition," or adding moisture/oil to a dry substance to nourish it.</note>, and subliming; **Fixation**, however, happens through marrying, resolving, and coagulating.

...the Stone, with the purified and subsequently reduced Mercury, can best be freed from its earthiness and moisture through the method of sublimation. It must be ground twice with this Mercury and subsequently buried in Mary’s Bath <note>original: "Balneo Mariæ"; a double boiler or water bath used for gentle heating in alchemy.</note>, as shall be explained below.

## How is the Mercury Purified and Cleansed?

Accordingly, the art of removing the superfluous earthy essence is this: sublimate it two or three times with vitriol <term>vitriol</term><note>A historical term for sulfate minerals, used here as a reagent to help purify the metal.</note> and salt, until you have its whitest essence before you. But when it rises very white into the heights <note>During the process of sublimation, the substance vaporizes and settles at the top of the vessel.</note>, then throw it into boiling water until it turns back into quicksilver <note>mercury</note>. Afterward, remove the water from it and work with it; for it is not good to work with it if it is not first purified in this manner.

Therefore Avicenna <note>A famous Persian polymath whose writings were fundamental to medieval European alchemy.</note> says: The beginning of making the "First" is that the Mercury be sublimated; thereafter, dissolve the same so that it returns to its first matter, and sublimate it entirely. Then place pure bodies, which have been correctly weighed, into this pure Mercury. Nevertheless, you must not mix the white body with the red, nor the red with the white; rather, dissolve each one separately into parts, because the white water serves to give the white color, and the red serves to give the red color. 

Accordingly, you must not mix the water of one Stone with the water of another, or with any other Stone, because you would err greatly and become quite blinded if you did otherwise. Thereupon, grind it one time after another, moisten it, and cook it in Mary’s Bath. Afterward, distill it through a distilling glass <note>A glass vessel used for heating and condensing vapors.</note> as long as it takes to pass through; however, collect the black matter floating on top bit by bit, because it is the "oil" and the true sign of dissolution. For that which has been dissolved comes all the way to the top; therefore, that which rises and seeks higher places—namely the golden body—is separated. But preserve it carefully, so that it does not fly away in the smoke...

...and what you do with the **White**, you must also do with the **Red**, because this Medicine is essentially the same in its nature; likewise, it is the same in its manner and way of working. Nevertheless, in the **Red** there is an addition of yellow color, because the essence of the fixed sulfur is made entirely pure. However, there is a difference between the **Solar** and **Lunar** Medicine <note>Solar medicine refers to the goal of creating gold (associated with the Sun); Lunar medicine refers to silver (associated with the Moon).</note>, because the former indeed encompasses the latter, but the latter does not; this is because it [the Lunar] requires the very purest white sulfur, just as the former [the Solar] requires the red. These two bodies are sufficient, for they resemble what is sought, or that which you seek; however, you have cause to apply yourself with effort to the dissolution, sublimation, and refinement. For they are strong and require a lengthy preparation and continuous operation so that they are first calcined <term>calcined</term><note>Reduced to a powder through intense heat.</note> and thereafter dissolved. Because once they have been calcined, they are easily dissolved; the heat of the fire, which penetrates the parts of the body, allows the water to enter therein, and thus it accepts the dissolution more readily. Nevertheless, when you calcine a strong body which can also be dissolved, set each part of it aside; and whatever remains in the distilling glass, take that away very cautiously so that it does not vanish into smoke, and thus the Art be in vain.

Therefore, because such things are difficult to perform, it is better to dissolve the strong bodies through the water alone—that is, through the quicksilver <note>mercury</note>—without calcination, because this is safer, even though the operation proceeds somewhat more slowly. You must therefore be patient and not extract the tincture in haste, nor seek to complete the work in a quick rush; for the first error in this Art is haste, because it burns everything and leads one toward a completely incorrect result. For if you provide too much fire at the beginning of the mixing, the tinctures will suffer damage, as the medicines are burned by excessive heat. From this come the verses:

### Recapitulation of the First Regime.

Now I wish to briefly report the entire manner and method of the dissolution: therefore, first sublimate the <term>Mercury</term> <note>The fluid, volatile principle in alchemy, often represented by quicksilver.</note>, and afterward you may dissolve it with the whole Earth and Fire; likewise, cook these things until they return into their <term>First Matter</term> <note>original Latin: *prima materia*; the primal, formless state of all things.</note>. This is done so that we may obtain the <term>Sulfur</term> <note>The active, combustible principle in alchemy.</note> and Mercury from that very matter out of which gold and silver are made beneath or under the earth. For if true Sulfur and Quicksilver were present, we could well make gold and silver from them. Whoever possesses this Art has an eternal treasure; however, three things are required for this Art: namely, a subtle understanding on the part of the artist, the operation of the hands <note>Actual laboratory practice and manual labor.</note>, and a free power and will—which in turn requires wealth, wisdom, and books. Therefore, this Art belongs to no one except the rich, etc. <note>In alchemical literature, "the rich" often refers to those who are "rich in spirit" or possess the significant financial resources required to fund long-term experiments and procure rare materials.</note> And so much for the First Regime, which consists of how one should dissolve the Stone, etc.

### The Seventh Chapter.

The Second Regime consists of how one should wash or purify the Stone—namely, the Black, Corrupted, and Stinking <note>This refers to the *Nigredo* or "blackness" stage, where the matter decays and putrefies before it can be purified.</note>—so that it becomes very bright and clear, and is cleansed of its filth. The dry ones are Fire and Earth; the watery ones are Air and Water. The Fire thus eats and consumes what is found on the outside, because it destroys the filth of the waters through distilling, and <insert>it</insert> subtilizes the same through the mildness of the Air, also diminishing the coarse nature of the Stone through <term>Calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or ash.</note>, and also the salty nature of the Sulfur...

### The Division of the Stone through the four
### Elements.

Take therefore the Stone corrupted in such a manner, and after you have thereafter distilled the same according to the four elements and measured it equally by a gentle fire, take its water; thereafter make the fire gradually stronger until you have received the entire air mixed with the fire; but that which remains lying burnt on the bottom, that is black dry earth. Accordingly, a subtler separation occurs through the water, when they cannot endure the fire, than is brought out through the ash, when they can endure the fire. In such a manner, you must therefore divide the four elements, because the water must be drawn out from its moist essence, and not from another or others, because in the same there is a greater <term>Tincture</term> <note>The powerful essence capable of transforming and coloring base metals into gold.</note>; concerning the earth, however, you need not be concerned of what essence it may be, as long as it is firm. ## On the Washing of the Water.

But when you have divided the elements of the Stone, as we have said, then wash them by distilling the Air and the Water seven times, while strongly <term>calcining</term> <note>Heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a powder or "ash."</note> the Fire and the Earth; however, you must distill the Water and the Air separately, because the Air is better than the Water, although the Water washes the Earth and makes it white, and causes a marriage-bond of the Tinctures. ## On the Third Regime, which consists in Bringing Back.

The third regime consists in Bringing Back <note>original: *Zurückbringen*; also known as *imbibition*, this is the process of "feeding" the dry, calcined earth with liquid to restore its life</note>, namely the moist Water over the dry Earth, so that it may regain its lost moisture. But because the Earth is made of two bodies, and two elements are dry, hard, and stony, the Fire and the Earth agree in their dryness. Therefore, they must be prepared at the same time, because they share the same preparation. 

Thus, unite the strength of the Fire with the Earth after the extraction of the Air, and prepare them together for the sake of shortening the task, and also so that their mixing happens well, the preparation is not confused, one may well tincture the other, and they are not burned during the conflict of the fire. Therefore, it is far safer and more direct if one prepares them together. The preparation of these, however, occurs so that they [attain] a greater moisture...

### That we should observe the specific quantity of each thing.

Now, if you wish to <term>prepare<note>original: "præpariren"; to treat a substance chemically to make it ready for the alchemical work.</note></term> our Stone, you should know that insofar as there is more water, air, fire, or earth within it after it has been <term>calcined<note>original: "calciniret"; reduced to a dry, crumbly state through intense heat.</note></term>, to that extent there will also be a greater dryness or a greater heat, a lesser cold or a lesser moisture within it. When it is dissolved, it is brought to a greater cold and lesser heat, to a greater moisture and lesser dryness. When it is <term>fixed<note>original: "figiret"; the process of making a substance stable or "firm" so that it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to heat.</note></term>, it is brought to a greater heat and lesser cold, to a greater dryness and lesser moisture.

Therefore, when the moist and the dry behold one another, the dry obtains from the moist that its parts are constrained—or continued—and can be easily poured; and the moist obtains from the dry that it holds the impression firmly and that it may endure all fire. ### On the Return of the Air over the Elixir to the White.

If not, then repeat the sublimation of the unfixed part over the same again and again until it can be quickly poured like wax without smoke.

Throw then one pound of it over 1,000 parts of *mercury* <note>original: "Mercurii"; quicksilver.</note> dissolved with salt in vinegar, and it will become the purest silver—even better than that from the mountain veins <note>referring to silver ore found in natural mines.</note>. Likewise, if any of it is thrown upon any imperfect body, that body will be transformed into the truest silver. 

The methods of the *composition* <note>original: "Composition"; the specific recipe or arrangement of ingredients.</note> of this truest *elixir* I have set before you in a perfect discourse, by means of which you will doubtless be able to attain it. Therefore, investigate it carefully, practice the methods of the governance <note>original: "Regierung"; the "regimen," or the precise control of the furnace's heat over time.</note> diligently, and you will find the power of it most clearly; which is accomplished neither by itself nor by chance—namely through miracles—but through the art in the *operation* <note>original: "Operation"; the practical, manual laboratory work.</note>. Thus, operate in whatever you wish, for I can give you no other counsel than this.

### On the Composition of the Red Elixir.

In the same way, the red *elixir* <note>original: "Elixir"; the legendary substance sought by alchemists to transform base metals into gold.</note> is also prepared for *Gold* <note>original: "Sole"; the Latin name for the Sun, representing Gold.</note>, just as the white was for *Silver* <note>original: "Luna"; the Latin name for the Moon, representing Silver.</note>, except only that for every white substance, one must take a red one; and instead of the powder of *Silver* <note>original: "Lunæ"</note>, one must take the powder of *Gold* <note>original: "Solis"</note>, and the water of *Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurii"; also known as quicksilver</note>, which has previously been made red by means of the fire of the stone. For in the red work, nothing must enter except what is red, just as in the white work, nothing enters but what is white. For in the *preparation* <note>original: "Præparation"</note> of the solar *medicine* <note>original: "Medicin"; alchemists often viewed their elixirs as healing agents that "cured" base metals of their impurities.</note>, which does not burn away, there is an addition of red sulfur in a stabilizing and *calcining* <note>original: "calcinirenden"; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter and reduce it to a powder.</note> manner in three parts of the prepared *ferment* <note>original: "Fermenti"; a catalyst substance used to "leaven" or trigger the transformation of the metal.</note> administered with great diligence and care, after various types of dissolution and *sublimation* <note>original: "Sublimation"; a process where a solid turns into gas and back to solid, used for purification.</note> with many repetitions, until that which is not *fixed* <note>original: "Fixirte"; a substance that has become stable and resistant to heat.</note> is made solid with that which is fixed at the bottom. Because the manner of this dissolution and stabilization happens through the repetition of the sublimation of the remaining unfixed part, which must be skillfully united with the fixed part even in its smallest pieces, until it is elevated with it and once more *transformed* <note>original: "figuret"; shaped or structured chemically.</note> with it so that it remains stable. When, however, three parts of its red water have been sublimated in this way one time after another with the same [fixed part] until it becomes solid at the bottom, then place it in a very hot fire for a night and a day, so that it might be better purified and made stable within it. Thereupon take it out and *refine* <note>original: "subtilisire"</note> it in a *crucible* <note>original: "Crucibulo"; a heat-resistant container used for melting metal.</note> over a gentle fire with its red oil, by dripping one drop after another over it, until it can be poured like wax without smoke, which remains with it and penetrates deeper, and also *tinges* <note>original: "tingiret"; the alchemical process of coloring or permanently changing a metal's essence.</note> and persists. Therefore, cast one pound onto one thousand parts of *Silver* <note>original: "Lunæ"</note> or *Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurii"</note> that has been washed with salt and vinegar, and it will become the truest *Gold* <note>original: "Sole"</note>, which withstands every test and is far better than that brought forth from the earth, because the silver and gold of this *elixir* far surpass the gold and silver from the earth in all fine properties.

## How You Must Understand Dissolution and Sublimation.

Nevertheless, you must not think that I am teaching a dissolution here in which the elixir is completely and utterly returned to water, but rather that you refine <note>original: "subtilisirest"; to break a substance down into its most basic, pure, or "subtle" essence.</note> it as much as you can, and separate its parts that were united during the fixation, and transform its dryness into moisture, and the strong into the simple. The refinement of these is a dissolution into the water, because distillation or dissolution brings the stone from potentiality <note>original: "Potentia"; a philosophical term meaning the capacity to become something else.</note> to the actual effect, because it makes it entirely subtle. Therefore, when the bodies are completely refined, the spirits are united with them altogether and cannot be separated from one another again by any kind of invention, because the fixation of the spirits <note>original: "Spirituum"</note> with the bodies then occurs when the bodies are subtle enough that they can retain the spirits within themselves. 

And therefore, whoever is able to separate the bodies at the first refinement will achieve the convenient and desired end, because the entire intention of the working artist should be directed toward how the spirits may be united with the bodies. And the union of the spirits and the bodies happens when the bodies are refined, so that the spirits and the bodies are refined through grinding <note>original: "Zerreibung"</note> and roasting <note>original: "Bratung"</note> them with the spirits. # Short Contents of Lacinius regarding Saint Raymond Lull, which he himself calls an Abridged Letter.

If I could benefit the lovers of this excellent art <note>The "excellent art" refers to alchemy.</note> as much as I would like, I would now bring all the works of Saint <term>Raymond Lull</term> <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315) was a philosopher and mystic; a large body of alchemical work was later attributed to him, though likely written by followers.</note> to light for the sake of instructional accuracy; but since I cannot do what I want, it is necessary that I do what I can. However, since among all of Lull's works, the one he sent to King Robert <note>Robert of Anjou, King of Naples (1275–1343), a common dedicatee of medieval alchemical texts.</note> as an epistle can be no less pleasant than fruitful and useful to many—being especially brief and clear, and according to the judgment of all the wise, perfect in every part—I could by no means allow myself not to share this *Compendium* <note>original: "Compendii", meaning a summary or abridgment.</note>, along with the works of Bonus and Rainaldo <note>Petrus Bonus and Rainaldus are other influential alchemical authors often grouped with Lull.</note>, with all students of the art. For in this very work, one can clearly recognize Raymond's entire intention in brief speeches. This little treatise is a short summary (as he himself calls it) of all his works; and since nearly everyone takes pleasure in brevity, I will explain the short treatise with words as brief as possible, after I have briefly recounted it.

In the first distillation, take only one and a half parts, and put this part back in for distillation; then take a fourth part of it and distill it for a third time. From this, take 2 parts again, and in the fourth distillation, take slightly less than the whole. Continue distilling this same part until the eighth or ninth time. After this, you must have two vessels made in the manner that "twins" <note>original: *Zwillinge*; likely a circulatory vessel like a "pelican," where vapors from two connected containers can flow back and forth</note> are depicted, each of which must have its lid attached. In one lid, there must be the craftsmanship that allows it to fit into the vessel. They must be of equal thickness—namely, the width of a flat hand. The reason for this is so that they can be set firmly against one another. Then, place one pound of this water into each vessel, along with an ounce of the **ferment** <note>original: *Fermento*; a catalyst used to trigger the transformation of the base material</note>, which has been very well purified and thinned into leaves. 

You must also have a masterfully crafted furnace where a charcoal fire can communicate only a tempered, uniform, and continuous heat through the "arms" of the furnace itself. Place your vessels there and light a fire; it is the most excellent art that the fire cannot be made greater than is necessary. For then, as soon as the vessels feel the heat, the **ferment** will be dissolved immediately. Then, tie a sponge around the tubes of the lid; these tubes should be wide and thick enough around the lid, but where they enter the vessels, they should be narrow. Keep a constant watch over these sponges, ensuring they are always moistened with fresh water <note>The wet sponges act as a cooling system to condense the rising vapors back into liquid</note>.

# A Short Summary of Raymond.

...world <note>This continues the thought from the previous page regarding the "Vegetable Way."</note> to be filled with this vegetable salt of his, which he often calls **Vegetable Mercury** <term>Mercurium vegetabilem: a specialized alchemical solvent believed to possess "living" or life-giving properties unlike mineral acids</term>, **Water of Life** <note>original: *Aquam vitæ*</note>, **Solvent** <note>original: *Menstruum*</note>, and **Menstrual Blood** <note>original: *Sanguinem menstruum*; a symbolic term for a primary dissolving agent in the alchemical "womb"</note>. He says that it has the properties of a body and is brought forth from the seed, as if from a woman; it is both generative and nourishing, and it causes hard things—namely gold and silver—to grow, bringing them to their actual essence until they are transformed into the **Stone** <note>The Philosopher’s Stone</note>. 

Therefore, if it makes gold and silver grow, it is clear that this occurs by means of their dissolution. Consequently, it dissolves the **Bodies** <note>the alchemical term for metals</note>, which must first be naturally **calcined** <term>calciniret: the process of reducing a metal to a fine powder through intense heat</term>, dissolved, and brought into the nature of spirits. He then calls these **foliated** <note>original: *foliata*; refers to a layered or leaf-like crystalline structure</note>. However, this work does not happen by means of some growing plant matter, as many fools believe, but rather it happens with things of its own kind, as Raymond himself demonstrates at great length in his *Codicil* <note>original: *Codicillo*; one of the most famous works of the Lullian alchemical corpus</note>. 

Therefore, Raymond says here that the entire path of minerals consists of two waters: one of which makes the Stone volatile <note>original: *flüchtig*; able to be evaporated or "flee" the fire</note>. I have already told you in the preceding pages that alchemists call "the Stone" that which does not evaporate in the fire. It is therefore necessary to make such a stone volatile, and then to **fix** <term>fixiren: the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat</term> it with another water, which will also be fixed by itself, as he himself says here. He states that this **Quintessence** <note>the "fifth essence" or purest part of a substance</note> of his is fixed with the **Ferment** <term>Fermento: a substance, often gold or silver, added to the alchemical mix to "leaven" the matter and trigger its final transformation</term>. For the Quintessence, which composes the entire Stone—at least as far as its nature and its **Tincture** <term>Tinctur: the transformative power or "dye" that allows the Stone to change base metal into precious metal</term> are concerned—is fixed and strengthened according to the ferment added to it, because it causes the transformation by virtue of that same ferment.

Nevertheless, the Quintessence could be fixed over its own earth and united with the metal, but this does not please Raymond. For if it is fixed over another ferment, be it simply "A" or "B" <note>likely referring to specific stages or substances labeled in a diagram in the original manuscript</note>, then the work happens more quickly, and its effect will be stronger and also more natural.

## *Collectanea Lacinii* or brief *Excerpts* from the book of *Rhazes*, called the *Light of Lights*. <note>Janus Lacinius was a 16th-century editor of alchemical texts; Rhazes (Rhasis) refers to the 9th-century Persian scholar Abu Bakr al-Razi, though the "Light of Lights" is a later Latin alchemical work attributed to him.</note>

Because the root of the science which is called *Alchemy* <note>original: *Alchymia*</note> consists primarily in *solution* <term>Solution: the process of dissolving a solid substance into a liquid state</term> or dissolving; therefore, one must apply oneself to know what exists in nature that can dissolve everything and then, once it has been dissolved, can *coagulate* <term>Coagulation: the process of turning a liquid back into a solid form</term> it once again. For unless all natural things are converted into vapor and steam, one will labor in vain in this art regarding them, by virtue of their own natural constitution; but when it is presented to the eyes in a dissolved state, an artist will derive manifold pleasure from it. From this it stems that the *philosophers* <note>the "philosophers" is a standard term for ancient alchemical authorities</note> say the whole art consists in dissolution and *coagulation*, as well as in the *operation* <term>Operation: the practical lab work or experimental procedure</term>. If we therefore wish to reach the highest summit of science here, we must *practice* what is dissolved in this science. Thus, with divine granting, we wish to speak of the vitriols <note>original: *Atramentis*; metallic sulfate minerals often used for their acidic properties</note>, the alums <note>original: *Aluminibus*; astringent mineral salts</note> which have the power of the same, of the mineral spirits, of the metals, and of the precious stones themselves. What their nature is, how and in how many ways they can be dissolved and *coagulated* so that they become perfect, we wish to diligently reveal to an understanding person and *practitioner* <note>original: *Operirenden*</note>; therefore, we also wish to instruct those who [seek] the *tinctures* <term>Tincturen: substances or elixirs used to change the properties of metals or used as powerful medicines</term>

### Concerning the Spirits.

There are, however, three mineral <term>spirits <note>In alchemy, "spirits" are substances that are volatile and can be easily vaporized by heat.</note></term>: Mercury, Sulfur, and Arsenic. We must speak of all of them. And indeed, firstly of Arsenic. Arsenic is warm and dry, possessed of the greatest power and might, yet of little value. It is also capable of burning all other bodies, for it very easily burns ore and other things.

To that end, we wish to strive with all the Wise that we might bring it from a spiritual into a bodily essence. Just as it does not endure in the fire but rather flees from it, we wish to work toward the goal that it remains within the fire and never flees from it; and that, while it remains, it gives a color to those things which are likewise mixed with it. It is to be known that it has a great affinity with vinegar, and when boiled with it after salt has been mixed in, it passes from its spiritual into a bodily essence.

## Of Sulfur.

Consequently, we must speak of sulfur <note>original: "Schwefel"</note>. And it should be known that sulfur accepts exactly the same kinds of boilings and in the same manner as arsenic. For sulfur itself is strongly changed through boiling with vinegar and salt; it also accomplishes much when it is boiled in oils. But because sulfur, in its heat and dryness, has a "windy" essence <note>Likely referring to volatile gases or an airy quality that makes the substance difficult to stabilize.</note> mixed in, it is not easily sublimated. Nevertheless, one should not concern oneself if it cannot be sublimated. Strive, therefore, to boil it well, and after it has been boiled, to dissolve it; thus, in your <term>terms <note>original: "Terminis"; the specific boundaries, stages, or theoretical limits of the alchemical process.</note></term>, the work will surpass all other works; for just as the philosophers <note>The "Philosophi" or "Philosophers" usually refers to the ancient and medieval alchemical authorities like Hermes Trismegistus or Geber.</note> have said, it is this very thing that makes gold with mercury; and if you understand what follows, when you bring it to perfection—that is, to true boiling and true dissolution—you will complete your work. These three things alone will be enough for you, and I advise you to keep them hidden.

# Collectanea from Rhazes. <note>original: "Rhasi"; referring to the 9th-century Persian alchemist and physician Al-Razi, known in Latin as Rhazes.</note>

Silver and gold cannot be made without these same substances. Some have said that if sulfur <note>original: "Schwefel"</note> is mixed with quicklime <note>original: "lebendigen Kalck"</note>, it can easily be <term>sublimated <note>The process of heating a substance so it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification.</note></term> with it. However, I do not wish for you to labor in vain; for if you do what I have commanded you, it will be sufficient for you. This one thing you should know: that arsenic <note>original: "Arsenicum"</note> is especially suitable for silver, but sulfur is for gold. For sulfur is white on the outside and red on the inside. In arsenic, however, the opposite is found, as can be seen during the operation.

If you want white sulfur to be red, dissolve it in red water <note>A common alchemical term for acidic or metallic solutions, often associated with vitriol or "the blood of the dragon."</note> through crushing, moistening, and thorough boiling. After it has been dissolved, <term>congeal <note>original: "congelire"; to solidify or crystallize a liquid substance.</note></term> it into a stone; and after it has been congealed, dissolve it once more with red water and congeal it again. For the third time, dissolve it with that same red water and sublimate it entirely through a strong fire. That which rises to the height like a dust is entirely white sulfur; but that which remains lying at the bottom is red-dyed sulfur, just like scarlet <note>original: "Scarlatum"</note>, and this is the best sulfur according to Aristotle <note>original: "Aristotele"; alchemical texts frequently cited Aristotle to lend authority to their processes, often drawing from apocryphal works.</note>. This sulfur will transform mercury into the truest gold through no small art.

## Of Mercury.

## Concerning Gold.

Concerning gold, the philosophers say that gold is an effect of the
Sun; for this reason, they consider it to be well-tempered <note>original: "wohl complexionirt"; referring to the four humors/qualities being in perfect balance.</note> in its
qualities. When it is perfectly purified, it suffers no loss in the fire,
but rather receives its color from the fire. Some have claimed that
gold can be manufactured through Art <note>In alchemy, "Art" refers to human chemical intervention as opposed to natural processes.</note>; however, Nature makes nothing
more from gold, nor does Art alter its essence. One thing I tell you:
if you wish to make gold, it is necessary that you ferment the gold.
If you do not ferment it, you will attempt all its work in vain.
Moreover, for there to be a <term>fermentum</term> <note>a substance (often gold or silver itself) added to "ripen" or transform a base metal into a noble one.</note>, and for any operation of it to
be valid, it must be pure. Because it is the purest thing in its own
nature, very little is sufficient for it to be further purified; for it does
not need much washing, as it is a sufficiently beautiful and pure
matter. Instead, it only needs to be prepared so that it can be
incorporated and fermented; however, it must first be <term>calcined</term> <note>reduced to a powder through intense heat.</note>,
as will be seen below.

All of this, however, will be accomplished by that powder / which makes the gold and silver fit to be hammered and sweet / when it is burned and <term>calcined <gloss>reduced to a dry powder through prolonged heating</gloss></term>. Take <term>sal ammoniac <gloss>ammonium chloride, often used as a flux or to "cleanse" metals</gloss></term>, <term>saltpeter <gloss>potassium nitrate, a powerful oxidizing agent</gloss></term>, and <term>borax <gloss>a mineral used as a flux to help metals melt and flow</gloss></term>, an equal amount of each / and crush it very well / and mix it together / and dissolve it in a little wine / and let it become dry / and add the powder of the aforementioned three things—one part to three parts—of whichever <term>calx <gloss>the oxide or "ash" of a metal remaining after it has been roasted in fire</gloss></term> you wish / and thus it will allow itself to be worked very well under the hammer.

Therefore consider and see what I shall tell you, etc.

How then shall we answer this? Shall we conclude, according to <term>Rhazes</term>, that the Art is not truthful but only deceptive? Especially since he himself says in the preceding chapter on gold that the gold which has been made in the manner he himself teaches is pure and irreproachable gold. This will be easily answered. We say, therefore: If you wish to know the whole work, then read the whole work; for he himself resolves this doubt in the chapter on ore, when he says: for copper is not called the <term>ferment <gloss>a substance, like yeast in bread, that was believed to "ripen" base metals into gold</gloss></term> (or something else—add this yourself—of the imperfect ones), because the <term>intention</term> of this art is not to make copper out of gold or silver, but on the contrary; for which reason he adds in the said place: Thus, when copper is washed, <term>calcined</term>, dissolved, etc., it will yield a color similar to gold, yet it will not be gold, because the seeds of things are found nowhere except in their own proper <term>species <note>original Latin: "speciebus"</note></term>; therefore <note>original Latin: "Ergo"</note>, no <term>ferment</term> can be made from imperfect things; therefore, there can also be no true transformation.

### Of the Ore or Copper.

The **copper** is prepared in the same way / as is the silver / but it has not been so purified / and not quite so **tempered** and **digested** / but it is, as it were, burnt / warm and dry. ### Of Lead.

Lead, however, is made in the same way / just as the other imperfect metals. ## Of Tin.

The body of tin is composed / just like <term>Saturn</term> <note>original: "Saturnus"; the alchemical name for lead.</note>, of moderately purified mercury and impure sulfur. It is white / but impure / of weak <term>digestion</term> <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the process of maturing a substance through gentle, continuous heat, similar to how the stomach processes food.</note>, and among all metals of various composition, all too dry and porous / which one can perceive from its crackling and hissing <note>This refers to the "cry of tin," a distinctive crackling sound made when a bar of tin is bent, caused by the internal crystal structure shifting.</note>. One must, however, purify it in the same way / as was said before regarding Saturn / a fourth part of mercury and a third of lead takes the crackling and hissing away from it. One must, however, moisten it with a <term>rectified oil</term> <note>An oil that has been purified and concentrated through distillation.</note> / or with distilled pig’s blood / until, after the moisture is consumed, it takes the hissing and crackling away from it. It must be purified, however / just like Saturn, with burnt salt / and through the boilings with salt and vinegar / and must be moistened with rectified oils / until it becomes wet / and loses the hissing. Rhazes, however, says / that it can hardly be brought to perfection / so that gold and silver might be made from it through any purification. For it blackens so much / that it spoils other metals / with which it is joined / and hardly any good mixture can happen with it; and if anyone tries this / he will be assured by experience / just like those / who have tried it.

### Of Iron.

Iron is composed—just like the other metals—of sulfur and mercury, both of which are coarse and impure. However, it transforms into steel, which is indeed of no other kind than iron. Into silver or gold, however, it can hardly or never be transformed. It can, however, be cast with white lead <note>Likely referring to ceruse or a lead-based flux.</note> alone, or with the aforementioned powder, which brings the <term>calxes</term> <note>original: "Kalche"; metallic oxides produced by heating a metal in air.</note> to the metals; but after casting, it cannot be hammered. Its usefulness, however, is even greater once the <term>crocus</term> <note>original: "Crocus"; a reddish-yellow powder or calcined metal, specifically "Crocus Martis" (iron oxide).</note> has been extracted from it, which has a permanent color for the work of <term>Sol</term> <note>original: "Solis"; the alchemical name for gold.</note>; but how the crocus is to be extracted is explained in another place, and there are a thousand ways to do so.

## *Collections of Lacinus* <note>Referring to Janus Lacinus, a 16th-century editor of alchemical texts.</note> from *Albertus Magnus*, Saint *Thomas*, and other *Authors* who are not available everywhere.

Most <term>philosophers</term> <note>original: "Philosophi"; here referring specifically to alchemists.</note> teach how one should prepare the various types of <term>medicines</term> <note>original: "Artzneyen"; in alchemy, these are the elixirs or tinctures used to transmute metals.</note>, and although at first glance they seem to be different, this only appears so to those who consider everything only superficially. For they all seem to be in agreement on one point; and first, Hermes, the father of the wise, says that the dissolved body is the eternal water, and it congeals the <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurium"; quicksilver.</note> through perpetual <term>congelation</term> <note>original: "Congelation"; the process of solidifying or thickening a substance.</note>. Similarly, another says: Prepare the bodies and dissolve them, and with this same water, moisten the washed <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "Spiritus"; volatile substances like sulfur or arsenic.</note>; then the spirits themselves are turned into <term>bodies</term> <note>original: "Corpora"; solid, stable substances.</note>, and the bodies into spirits, and thus the spirits are fixed with the bodies themselves through a firm <term>fixation</term> <note>original: "Fixion"; the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note>. Similarly, Rhazes says: Turn the bodies into water, and unite the same

### Collections from various Authors.

Water with <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurio"; here referring to the alchemical principle of fluidity and transformation.</note>, and from both of these make a water once again. Likewise, another says: If you do not dissolve the bodies, you labor in vain. From this comes the verse:

->If you dissolve the fixed, and make the dissolved fly,<-
->And you turn back the flying one.<-
->If you join these three, they will make you live safely.<-
<note>original Latin: "Si fixum solvas, faciasque volare solutum, / Et volucrem volvas. / Hæc tria si jungas facient te vivere tutum." This is a classic alchemical maxim describing the "Great Work": dissolving a solid (solutio), vaporizing it (sublimatio), and then fixing it back into a solid (coagulatio).</note>

That is: If you dissolve the solid and make it so that the dissolved becomes volatile, and turn the volatile back again. If you unite these three things, they will cause you to live in safety. Likewise, another says: You who carry a longing for the gift of **God**, contemplate the lovely spring of this matter. I command you in plain words that you transform the non-flowing and dripping water into the <term>Moon</term> <note>original: "Lunam"; the alchemical name for silver.</note> and the <term>Sun</term> <note>original: "Solem"; the alchemical name for gold.</note>. This is the first rare root, which is given to us and is very precious, according to the testimony of **Hermes** <note>original: "Hermetis"; Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of the hermetic and alchemical tradition.</note>. Therefore, **Albertus** <note>original: "Albertus"; Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a prominent medieval scholar and saint whose name was often attached to alchemical texts.</note> himself says: Gather the various flowers which are full of the scent of all that is good. In which one can smell the sweetness and see the beauty, ornament, and glory of the world. This is the flower of all flowers, the rose of all roses, and the lily of the valley <note>original: "Meyen-Blume"; literally "May-flower," usually referring to the Lily of the Valley, used here as a metaphor for the refined alchemical substance.</note>. Thus rejoice, youth, in your youth, and learn to gather the flowers, because I have led you into the Garden of Paradise. So make from them a crown for your head, rejoice, and enjoy the delights of this world, while praising **God** and offering a helping hand to your needy neighbor. Now I will open to you the science or the secret, and I will make you understand the darknesses of this art; and what has long been hidden shall now be clearly revealed to you.

Therefore, **Albertus** teaches first to gather the flowers—that is, to purify the <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "Spiritus"; in alchemy, these are volatile substances that can be vaporized by heat.</note>; secondly, to make them solid through repeated <term>sublimation</term> <note>original: "Sublimation"; a purification process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then condensed back into a solid, leaving impurities behind.</note> in a protected vessel; further, to dissolve them; and finally, to <term>coagulate</term> <note>original: "coaguliren"; to turn a liquid or vapor back into a stable solid form.</note> them. Therefore, we shall speak of the purifications of the <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "Spirituum"; the plural form of spiritus.</note>, but first of them in general.

# Collectanea
<meta>catchword: First</meta>

### Of the *Spirits*.
<note>original: "Spiritibus"; in an alchemical context, "spirits" refer to volatile substances—vapors or essences—that are capable of penetrating and changing solid bodies.</note>

The pure bodies of the metals, after their preparation, are brought to perfection through the mineral *spirits*, whose purity and <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "Digestion"; the process of slow, continuous heating used to "cook" or mature a substance until it reaches perfection.</note> in the final degrees of perfection must provide the essence: so that within them there is a power to purify and to *digest*. These, however, are the *spirits* which have a natural power to animate and to transform; they are the elements of those things which can be extracted—that is, the <term>matter</term> of the metals and their <term>substance</term>, as the essence of that which is composed of elements. As a man of understanding, you should never wonder if a right well-purified and *digested spirit* transforms a large lump of metal. Although the *spirit*, when calculated against the *quantity* of the metal, is smaller, it is nonetheless greater because of its strong power, as it belongs to the spirit to act, but to the metal to be acted upon. For the *spirit* acts according to its own nature and according to its proper characteristics.

By virtue of its own nature, it acts against the body of the metal when it is united with it, as something that is more purified and *digested*, and which is more fiery and <term>subtle</term> <note>original: "subtil"; meaning finely divided, penetrating, or refined into a non-coarse state.</note>, and has less of *matter* but more of *form*. Because of such a difference in purification and *digestion*, there also follows a difference in the <term>species</term> <note>original: "Specierum"; the specific types or kinds of metals produced.</note> and kinds. It also acts according to its qualities, as is said in the <term>fourth book of Meteorology</term> <note>original: "quarto meteororum"; a reference to Book IV of Aristotle’s *Meteorologica*, which was the primary textbook for understanding the composition of minerals and the effects of heat and cold in the Middle Ages.</note>. In all things one can see a heat and a cold which define and transform both equal and unequal things, so that they are more active, etc. Of which he says further in the same place: If, however, the worthier work of these virtues in the natural generation and transformation of things belongs to *digestion*, yet so that the *spirit* may attain this power, one must purify and *digest* it in the best way, bring it into the body of the metal, and after it has been brought in, it must be constant and not depart. If you omit one of these three necessary parts, your endeavor will be in vain, and you will condemn your ignorance and negligence with tears.

# From various authors.
<note>original: "aus unterschiedlichen Autoribus."</note>

First, we must therefore deal with the **preparation of the spirits**, which is necessary in the Art. Regarding this preparation of the spirits, however, we have enough examples in the workings of Nature during the generation of metals. For in the natural generation of **gold**, the nature of the spirits is <term>sublimated</term> <note>original: "sublimiret"; the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then collecting the refined solid that forms as it cools.</note> by the heat of the **earth-vein**. There, it is found that the heat of the mineral vessel <note>The "mineral vessel" refers to the surrounding rock or geological structure that contains the ore.</note> in such veins of metals raises the sulfurous essence of the spirits far higher from the mineral vessel, and that the spirits themselves are found at the top, pure and clear, having been warmed and purified by their passage through the earth.

For the dry, heated earth warms the impurities and draws them to itself, consuming the superfluities; it retains and accepts the coarser parts, but the watery, airy, fiery, <term>subtle</term>, and purer parts—which evaporate due to the heat of the fire—rise to the heights. Therefore, the Art follows after Nature. And for this reason, artificial **sublimation** was invented, through which we purify the spirits with dry substances that consume superfluities, so that they remain for us entirely pure and bright—surpassing all the workings of Nature. This is because, in the wild, the course of Nature acts alone. 

With us, however, both the general and the specific course of Nature act together, because we work according to those things by which Nature works, and from which the power to act is already communicated here; and also according to those things which we, through the invention of Art, add to the naturally acting things, which are required so that one can work all the more quickly and better. For example: it happens that **iron** is generated in its vein, and it occurs according to the common course of Nature that its **sulfur** and its **mercury** must be <term>congealed</term> <note>original: "congeliret"; to be solidified or "frozen" into a fixed metallic state.</note> before they are purified. Nature, which does not contradict itself, did not prevent the incoming cold from reaching the matter that had not yet been purified, which would have congealed it too soon. ## On the Purifications of the Spirits.
<note>original: "Von den Reinigungen der Spirituum."</note>

Initially, we must speak of the purifications of the **spirits**, which must always take place so that the superfluous things—which are necessary outside of <term>corruption</term> <note>original: "Corruption"; here referring to the chemical breakdown or putrefaction of matter required for transformation.</note>—are consumed. In some things, however, a threefold **spirit** is found: namely the **mineral**, **vegetable**, and **animal**. Therefore, we must speak of all of them. And indeed, first of the **mineral** ones, because common Nature works through them. 

Strictly speaking, there are three **mineral spirits**: sulfur, quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, and **arsenic**. These **operate** in the metals in a natural way, and the metals that have been prepared through the natural Art are united with them in a natural way. Among these, however, sulfur is the primary active principle <note>original: "das hauptsächlich Würckende"</note>, while quicksilver is the primary passive principle <note>original: "das hauptsächlich Leidende"; literally "the one that suffers or receives action"</note>, and **arsenic** oversees the secondary effects of the quicksilver. 

All three of these, however, come together in a **prepared** state during the completion of the **Elixir**; they retain the power of action over the **body** <note>original: "Cörper" / "Corpus"</note> of every passive metal. Sulfur, however, holds the highest place of action and transformation among these; therefore, it is to be treated first and foremost.

Sulfur is an oily **body**, composed of subtle earth and water, strongly moistened with an airy, fatty, and greasy moisture, which can be poured when heated but allows itself to be **coagulated** <note>original: "coaguliren"; to thicken or set into a solid form</note> when it becomes cold. It is the **material** part of all metals during the process, just as it is itself the active principle...

->On Arsenic.<-

After we have brought the treatise on mercury to an end, we must now deal with arsenic. Arsenic, however, is a mineral body / composed of earth and water / which are strongly mixed with one another: it is indeed oily, like sulfur / yet it does not have such an abundance of oil / as it does of earth / and because of the sulfur it is thicker and more earthy. Its purification, however, occurs by means of the first <term>sublimation</term> <note>the process of heating a substance until it becomes a vapor and then collecting the solid that forms when it cools, used to purify chemicals</note> / so that one sublimates it with drying things that consume its oily essence / which is the first moisture / as well as the superfluous watery essence / which is the other evaporating moisture.

In the name of **GOD**, take light, heavy, red, or yellow arsenic <note>likely referring to realgar (red) and orpiment (yellow), which are natural arsenic ores</note>, and crush it very small / along with an equal weight, and half as much again, of copper filings or iron <term>slag</term> <note>original: "Schlacken"; the stony waste matter separated from metals during smelting</note> / and moisten it with vinegar / and incorporate and dry it well / and set it along with its dregs for sublimation between two layers of the powder / with which it is sublimated / one finger thick in circumference. And thus apply fire / as long as until the moist smoke ceases / then close it up / and <term>lute</term> <note>seal a vessel with airtight clay or cement</note> the vessel well / and at first apply a strong fire / and afterwards the strongest fire of all / until it is entirely sublimated: afterwards let it cool / and gather together / what appears outside of the dregs / and mix it with new dregs and powders / and sublimate it once more / as before / until it is white and pure / bright and crystalline / after all moisture and superfluity have been consumed. Upon mercury, the prepared sulfur works in this manner: Take one pound of quicksilver <note>original: "Mercurii vivi"</note>, five pounds of purified cast Jupiter <note>tin</note>, and put these together; pulverize it entirely in a marble mortar with an equal amount of common roasted salt. Stir it together for a long time with a wooden pestle, without any moisture, until the salt becomes very black. Afterwards, wash it with "sweet" <note>fresh or pure</note> water as often as needed until all the blackness is removed. Finally, after you have added as much salt to it, you shall roast it over a gentle fire; rub this together in an earthen dish for an hour so that the salt becomes dry. When the mercury begins to "fly" <note>evaporate or sublimate</note>, put it into a mortar as before and crush it very well, until the salt, which has become very black from the sulfurous moisture and blackness, is drawn out from it.
