## How the aforementioned sulfur works upon Venus.

After we have seen how one must use the sulfur upon <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurio"; the alchemical name for quicksilver</note> and <term>Jupiter</term> <note>original: "Jove"; the alchemical name for tin</note>, we must also see how the same must be used upon <term>Venus</term> <note>original: "Venere"; the alchemical name for copper</note>: Take <term>Venus</term>, and specifically that which is prepared just as was said of the <term>Venus</term> that is to be prepared; pour it, and after it has been poured, throw over the same the tenth part of the aforementioned sulfur, so that immediately something yellow will emerge. Then lay it upon rods that have been dipped in pig's blood; thus you will find that <term>Venus</term> has been almost transformed into the property of <term>Luna</term> <note>original: "Lunæ"; the alchemical name for silver</note>, in that it has the white color of <term>Luna</term> entirely, or at least nearly so, as well as the sweetness <note>a term for malleability and smooth flow</note> during pouring and hammering, and a good <term>composition</term>, so that one does not perceive the fiery essence. This is a secret word <note>a phrase indicating a significant or veiled alchemical truth</note>. Therefore, we wish to speak briefly of each, and indeed first

### Of Subtilization.

Subtilization is when certain things are moistened with a moisture, so that the parts may be better united, or also dissolved. Hence, it occurs for three reasons: first, so that one thing may be dissolved by the other, as when the *spirits* <note>Volatile substances like mercury or sulfur.</note> or *bodies* <note>Solid metals.</note> are moistened with the water of *sal armoniac* <note>original: "Salis armoniaci"; ammonium chloride, a salt used in alchemy to help dissolve metals and volatile substances.</note>. Secondly, so that they may be united, and one united thing may retain the other, as when the sublimated spirits are moistened with the waters of the bodies, which hold them back and are *fixed* <note>original: "figiret"; the alchemical process of making a volatile substance stable so that it no longer evaporates when heated.</note>. Thirdly, so that they may be better mixed and purified, which happens when the things, before they are yet sublimated, are moistened with a drying and penetrating moisture, such as common salt and the like.

### Of Sublimation.

Sublimation is when a thing is raised from the lower part of the vessel in which it is, through the air, into the upper part. And such occurs in three ways, or comes...

### Of Roasting.

**Roasting** <note>original: "Bratung"</note> means to dry the subtilized things—which have been placed in a glass vessel and set over hot ashes—by the fire, while turning the vessel often, in the manner of a roast, and occasionally stirring the matter with a small rod.

### Of Calcination.

**Calcination** is the pulverization of a substance by fire, due to a lack of the moisture that consolidates the parts, which must necessarily occur in the Art. For no complete and perfect mixing of the bodies and the spirits occurs unless both are turned into water, which is the **first matter** <note>original: "erste Materie"; the primordial substance from which all metals were thought to originate.</note> of metals. This cannot happen as long as they possess their natural moisture, which causes them to be cast, melted, and moved in the fire in the manner of water, and which keeps the parts of the body together constantly and fixes them; and nothing can be mixed with them through which they could be turned into water. Therefore, it is necessary that such moisture be taken from them—

### Of Roasting.

**Roasting** means to dry out the subtilized substances—which have been placed in a glass vessel and set over hot ashes—by the fire, while frequently turning the vessel in the manner of roasting meat, and occasionally stirring the matter with a small stick.

### Of Calcination.

**Calcination** is the pulverization of a substance through fire, caused by a lack of the moisture that consolidates the parts, which must necessarily occur in the **Art** <note>The "Art" or "Great Work" refers to the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. For no complete and perfect mixing of the bodies and the spirits occurs unless both are turned into water, which is the **First Matter** <term>Materia Prima: the original, chaotic state of matter from which metals are formed.</term> of metals; this cannot happen as long as they possess their natural moisture, which causes them to be cast, melted, and moved in the fire like water, and which holds the parts of the body together and stabilizes them. Nothing can be mixed with them through which they might be turned into water [otherwise]. Therefore, it is necessary that such moisture be taken [away] from them...

<meta>catchword: away (men)</meta>

It emphasizes that calcination is necessary to remove "natural moisture," allowing solid bodies and volatile spirits to eventually be reduced to their "First Matter."</summary>

## Of Dissolution.
<note>original: *Von der Aufflösung*</note>

To dissolve means / to bring the calcined body back into water again / therefore three steps are necessary for this / namely to calcine the body itself / and when it has been calcined / to moisten it through subtilizing with dissolving water / and after it has been moistened / to dry it off by roasting / and afterwards to set it in a vessel in the place of dissolution / and after it has stood there for a long time / if something remains behind / that has not been dissolved / it must again be moistened with that which is dissolved / and this as often / until the entire body is dissolved in water. The way and manner of the dissolution is thus / that you make a pit in a damp place / or in a horse stable / which should be 2 cubits <note>original: *2. Ellen*; a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to the length of a forearm.</note> deep / and if the place is not sufficiently damp / then the pit itself must be doused with water / until it is thoroughly damp all over / thereafter take sand / scattering it in such quantity / as seems good to you / and pour water over it / until it is right damp / and place there the flask along with the moist substance / which is to be dissolved / or the medicine; thereafter seal the flask very well with wax / and over the wax put damp sand / and let it remain there for 7 or more days / if you wish / and so it will be dissolved into water. Others dissolve it differently / namely with a gentle fire in a *Balneum Mariae* <note>original: *Balneo Mariæ*; a "Mary's Bath" or water bath, used for providing consistent, gentle heat.</note>; others in a cold and damp place. Note / that you will not dissolve it as easily / as you would perhaps like—

### Of Distillation.

# A Curious Question Concerning the Nature of the Sun and Moon
## from Michael Scotus.

In order that the end may agree with its beginning in all parts, the question is asked: Whether one can make true gold according to the Art <note>The "Art" refers to alchemy, the precursor to modern chemistry.</note> or not? And it seems initially that it cannot happen, because gold, being itself a perfect body, requires a place of generation entirely its own, namely the body or the veins of the earth, just as wine requires the body of the vine. Therefore <note>original: *Ergo*</note> it cannot be made except in its own place. Likewise, no essential form <term>essential form <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "essential form" is the internal principle that makes a thing what it is; without it, the substance is merely raw matter.</note></term> can be brought there where actual active agents cannot be found to work upon actual passive subjects in an artificial way. Furthermore, the essential form of <term>Sol</term> <note>original: *Solis*; in alchemy, Sol represents both the Sun and the metal Gold.</note> does not arise from the warmth of the sun or of the fire used by such artists; rather, it originates from the [celestial] heat of the Sun: Therefore, etc <note>original: *Ergo &c.*</note>.

Regarding this question, it is to be known that nothing else is being asked but whether a seed-like power <term>seed-like power <note>original: *saamentliche Krafft*; alchemists believed metals grew in the earth like plants, and thus contained a "seed" or "sperm" that could be harvested and replanted.</note></term> can be produced in an artificial way from a mineral—namely <term>Sol</term> or <term>Luna</term> <note>original: *Sole oder Luna*; representing Gold and Silver.</note>—which would immediately and in an instant harden <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurium*; liquid quicksilver.</note> to the hardness of Gold. However, we wish to show this first by assuming that such a seed-like power is found; then it can be conveniently extracted from Gold, and is indeed extracted with rational arguments.

Secondly, it must be said how the power to sprout exists within Gold itself. Thirdly, it must be said how it is sown into the earth, and what kind of earth nourishes it—that is, how the sowing is multiplied. Fourthly, concerning the signs of the mineral power, which are brought into the living <term>Mercury</term> as identical <term>accidents</term> <note>original: *Accidentia*; in philosophy, "accidents" are the observable properties of a thing (like color or hardness) that are not part of its essential nature.</note>. Finally, all the [initial] arguments must be answered.

Regarding the first point, it is to be known that such a seed-like...
